title: How Trench Crusade tells some of the most exciting stories in miniature wargames
content:
Trench Crusade's unique blend of historic warfare and gruesome Catholic fantasy make it one of the most striking miniature wargames of recent years. Mike Franchina's delightfully nasty art opens the door to a world I'd hate to live in, but I'm desperate to explore. Those initial images are also backed up by some of the most enticing, entrail-laden lore in the modern hobby. What is it that makes it so damned exciting?

For the uninitiated, Trench Crusade takes place on an alternate Earth where Crusaders opened a Hellmouth in Jerusalem. For the next 800 years, demonic forces flooded the world and tried to take it from the faithful and mortal. The wars you know were waged, but this time, humanity fights the forces of Hell. Now, it's 1914, and the battle between Fallen and Faithful takes place in the trenches of No Man's Land.

Longtime wargamer Tim Linward says this is the best grimdark storytelling since early 2000s Games Workshop. Personally, I'm much newer to the world of wargames - but Trench Crusade compels me just the same. I find myself drawn to its gruesome sanctity, its gnarly monstrosities, and its portrayal of humanity - both horrid and holy.

That's why I jumped at the chance to chat with former Mordheim designer Tuomas Pirinen about Trench Crusade's deep, dark lore. Wargamer has asked Pirinen for all sorts of wisdom, from slick rules design to mentoring the next generation of wargame designers. Now, I have a new question: if God is real, what is Trench Crusade trying to tell him?

Pirinen's answer is personal rather than explicitly canon. He's written basically the entire timeline of Trench Crusade, and all the gory details in-between, but faith is a personal thing - even when it's in a fictional world.

"I believe that, in order for there to be free will, God can't just solve your problems", he tells me. "In the Trench Crusade universe, we are God's children, and you've got to let your children grow up and make their own mistakes. This war was started by humans opening the gates of Hell, by their own free will."

God, then, takes a hands-off approach in Trench Crusade. Even when the word of God powers Faithful troops, humanity has engineered it. Strange mutations and arcane machines fuel their forces, though the cost of that firepower is desecrating the temples we call mind and body. Pirinen tells me this is well within tradition for stories inspired by Christianity.

"Tolkien was extremely clear that The Lord of the Rings is a Christian, Catholic book", he says, "and yet God doesn't interfere". "Eru Ilúvatar, Tolkien's version of the Catholic God, isn't throwing thunderbolts or resurrecting people. But when Gollum betrayed Frodo at Mount Doom, he slipped, not because God pushed him, but because God built a world where a betrayal born from free will suffers the consequences."

Tolkien himself fought in World War One, though his whereabouts in the Trench Crusade canon remains unknown. It'll probably stay that way, too. While many real world figures feature, from Jean d'Arc to Catherine of Sienna, Pirinen doesn't want to simply repeat history.

"One of the most common questions we get is 'what about Napoleon?' 'What about the Red Baron?' 'What about Tolkien?' But if you do all that, it gets very gimmicky." "Plus, you need to do a lot of research, because we want to do justice to any character from real-world history. Then, it starts becoming not your world or your story."

Trench Crusade's roots in reality make it more affecting, Pirinen says, and he thinks that's one of the reasons the wargame has been such a runaway success. "When we show a map of the Trench Crusade world, everybody looks at what's happening at home - and you don't get that with a pure fantasy world", he tells me.

Still, Trench Crusade cherishes its creative freedom. It means the designers can explore the "fascinating history" of countries like Ukraine and Ethiopia, but free of real-world events like war, occupation, and colonialism that strip these nations of agency.

"That's much more interesting than repeating history", Pirinen says. "People who normally don't get featured in wargames get to have agency." "I'm super proud we have players in Turkey and Africa, which isn't common at all for a wargame", he adds, "so I want to explore these areas too."

Alternate histories aside, sometimes the truth is actually stranger than fiction. Take the throwing crosses you can wield as weapons. "We get a lot of people saying 'but this is a complete fantasy!'", Pirinen says "It's real. 100%. They were real weapons."

It's a careful balance of creativity and authenticity, but Trench Crusade nails it to a cross. Both are backed up by huge amounts of care and research. Real Catholic Clerics help craft the lore behind the wargame. Pirinen even interviewed veterans of the Finnish Civil War, so Trench Crusade's mechanics better represent the reality of Trench warfare.

"It isn't a simulation game, but I wanted you to actually feel like you're taking these daring dashes, throwing a grenade, and following up with a bayonet charge", he says. "I wanted the lore, art, miniature, and mechanics to fulfill the fantasy, exactly as imagined."

Dig underneath the interesting details, and you find what truly makes Trench Crusade lore compelling. It's a big question, one that's easy to empathize with: "When you are fighting the literal forces of Hell, how far can you go before you are indistinct from your enemies?"

Trench Crusade is a world where evil is real and tangible, and all humanity has banded together to resist it. But humans are far from righteous do-gooders. They mutilate themselves and others, use doctrine to manipulate, and even throw children into the line of fire. "Even if you're fighting a just war", Pirinen says, "it's easy to go too far."

These are the building blocks of a lore that truly enthralls. A profound premise, elevated by authentic real-world histories backed up by careful research. Throw in some of grimdark's most creative minis, art, and storylines, and you've got a world that, however horrific, I'm dying to enter.

Trench Crusade and its 10/10 Carcass Front box set, are currently available at Essen. I've even more stories to tell straight from the booth, so sign up to the Wargamer Discord to hear them first.

title: 11th Edition Detachment Focus: Paragons of Putrescence
content:
In our Detachment Focus series we take a deep dive into an army’s Detachments, covering what’s in them, how they play, and how they’ll fit into the broader meta and your games. In this Detachment Focus we’re looking at the Contagion Engines Detachment for the Death Guard.

The Death Guard received three new 1 DP Detachments at the onset of 11th edition, each of which catered to a different unit type in the army. Of these, the Paragons of Putrescence focuses on the army's CHARACTER units, and as a result acts as the Detachment with the widest use among those 1 DP options.

Detachment Cost: 1 DP

Force Disposition: Priority Assets

This is a character-focused Detachment, and that means it can pair with a large number of builds and Detachments, but will primarily favor those running Plague Marines or Terminators. Notably, you can pair this one with Champions of Contagion, and that means a bit more when you have both extra Contagion Range and the ability to customize/do more with your Contagion. This is also the ideal paired Detachment for Shamblerot Vectorium, where you want to get more out of your large units of Poxwalkers with attached characters and Mortarion. Giving you the Priority Assets Disposition is an added bonus there, since it stops you from having to play Disruption.

Detachment Rule: Hypervirulent Strains

Friendly DEATH GUARD CHARACTER units have +3” to their Contagion Range (to a max of 12”).

This is just a great buff to have on all the time, and gives you 6” range in the first battle round - that’s a lot to work with, and makes your job tagging units in those early turns way easier. This also works on Mortarion, giving the big guy an extra menacing aura to work with as he floats around the table. If you combine this with Death Lord’s Chosen you can get some silly range on your mortal wounds ability, and it’s solid when you’re doubling upon on Contagions in Death Lord’s Chosen. It's also fine on Poxwalkers led by characters, though you'll lose the ability to Infiltrate when you attach to those units, so the benefits are somewhat limited in that regard. Having 9" contagion range on round 2 can really make some nasty tricks possible, such as daisy chaining deep striking units of Deathshrouds.

Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Enhancements

  • Rejuvenating Swarm (20 points). Goes on a non-TERMINATOR INFANTRY model only. Attacks targeting this unit with S greater than their T have -1 to wound rolls. This is great for improving the durability of Plague Marines, where being T6 and having -1 to wound from bigger attacks is just a really solid buff on a unit that can be surprisingly fragile. You know where it's even better, though? On a unit of 20 Poxwalkers, where you can make them even more of a pain in the ass to pick up. -1 to wound is even better when it's on T4 models who are more likely to eat 3+ rolls.
  • Host of the Hybridised Pox (40 points). INFANTRY model only. Once per battle, per army, in your Command phase, you can use this ability. If you do, you pick one of the plagues in Nurgle’s Gift and until the end of the battle your unit gets that plague in addition to the one you chose. This is also pretty neat, and a fun way to get -1 to be hit on top of the -1 to saves from Rattlejoint Ague. It’s cute, but probably not worth spending points. That said, you can combine this with Cornucophagus in Champions of Contagion to have all three effects in play at once. For 40 points, this is just a bit too much to spend, and the reality is that the -1 to saves plague is really all you need.

Stratagems

  • Territorial Infection (1 CP). Used at the start of the Command phase on a CHARACTER unit to give that unit +1 OC until the end of the turn. This is a really great way to steal an objective, and particularly useful on Deathshroud Terminators, where a unit going from 4 OC to 8 can make a big difference, but can also be useful for getting Plague Marines up to 3 OC each. It’s a big brain play that can cause a lot of problems if your opponent isn’t ready for it and it can be used in your opponent’s turn. It's also amazing when you can throw it on a blob of 20 Poxwalkers to suddenly hold a crapload of table space and steal both middle objectives.
  • Aggravus Spasms (1 CP). Used at the start of your Shooting phase on a friendly Death Guard CHARACTER unit. Pick one visible enemy unit within Contagion Range of your unit and that unit gets +6” Detection range. This is interesting - it means you can tag a unit within 9” on round 2 and give it 21” Detection Range, but if you’re within 9” you’re already just going to light that unit up and/or charge it. It’s an interesting ability but I’m not sure how much you’ll actually use it. Helpful for those times when Poxwalkers are outkicking your coverage, usually when you're being supported by Defilers and/or a Knight.
  • Simultaneous Contamination (1 CP). Used in your Shooting phase, when a CHARACTER unit starts an Action. The unit can still shoot while it does the action. This is nifty, and handy if your plan is to play Priority Assets or for those rare turns you draw Cleanse or Plunder. Pretty situational otherwise, though. It only lets you shoot, so the value is going to be more around taking extra shots with your Malignant Plaguecasters or units of Plague Marines, or for when Mortarion needs to hang back.
Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Playing This Detachment

This is just a really versatile Detachment, and your go-to if you're running one of the other 2 DP options, as there's no world where you aren't taking at least a few characters. As we've mentioned, the most competitive way to use this Detachment is alongside Shamblerot Vectorium, where you get access to both Priority Assets - fine for an army running 7+ units of Poxwalkers - and the Rejuvenating Swarm Enhancement, which usually goes on a Noxious Blightbringer attached to a 20-model Poxwalkers unit alongside Typhus to create a nasty blob with extra movement, better healing, and added durability against incoming attacks. This is the current competitive list for Death Guard, and whether you play Priority Assets or Disruption will largely depend on whether you're playing in a Teams event (Teams events favor Disruption as this army does an OK job running it and someone has to jump on that particular grenade).

After that, you can get mileage out of Aggravus Spasms if you're being supported by Defilers or a Knight Despoiler, since it's about debuffing an enemy unit near one of your CHARACTER units - increasing a unit's detection range by 6" is quite a bit, and you can really open up on opponents who otherwise thought they were safe. Simultaneous Contamination is one that has limited utility given Poxwalkers can't shoot, but it's good to have in your back pocket for those times Mortarion wants to do an action and shoot and isn't in charge range of anything.

Strengths

  • Rejuvenating Swarm. This is a crazy good Enhancement and makes big units of Poxwalkers insanely annoying to try and take down.
  • Versatile. Buffing characters with extra contagion range is just always good, and you're always bringing characters.

Weaknesses

  • No real offensive buffs. Extra contagion range is nice but also not necessarily something you need, especially after round 3, and the real buff here is just a defensive buff you pay for on a single unit.

Final Thoughts

If you're running Death Guard competitively, chances are you're taking this one. It pairs wonderfully with Shamblerot Vectorium and the characters you want to take there, and gives you a much better disposition option. The Stratagems here are fine, the abilities solid, and most of your non-vehicle units are either characters or able to have attached characters, making this one that most of your army can use effectively.

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: Godeater's Son, by Noah van Nguyen
content:
credit: Black Library

With the release of Blood of the Godeater, let’s take a look at the first of Noah Van Nguyen’s books about the Chaos warlord, Heldanarr Fall.

Gentrification has hit Candip, an ancient and proud city in some hot dusty corner of Aqshy. The native tribes of the region, who had weathered the horrors of the Age of Chaos without giving into corruption, are struggling with the implications of the so-called Age of Sigmar.  Since the Azyrites burst back into the Realm of Fire, promising to reistablish civilisation, after fleeing to hide in Azyr while the dark forces ruled the realms, things haven't exactly been great.

On the face of it, Sigmarite devotees trying to reclaim the realms from the Dark Gods is a good thing, right?  But like a bunch of hipsters moving into a run-down, inner-city neighbourhood bringing with them their overpriced coffee shops, artisan beard barbers and yoga boutiques, the Azyrites carve out a nice little life for themselves at the expense of the Aqshyan locals, many of whom are no longer able to afford to live in their ancestral homeland because the cost of housing, food and, most importantly, booze, has increased so much.

Heldanarr Fall is a shit-farmer who has just about had enough of all this.  He sees the injustice that has befallen his people at the hands of the Azyrites, and watches as his people’s quality of life declines year on year.

He and his sister, Varrianala (Varry), are reduced to collecting the droppings, or magnure, of the areas native lavamanders, which they sell to the city’s wealthy to heat their homes with. To Fall, there is little difference between the followers of Chaos and the denizens of Order; both seek to rob him and his people of all they have, they just have different ways of doing it. All gods are let downs, no matter that pantheon they belong to.

But at least the Fall siblings have each other. When you don’t have a lot of much else (other than piles of lavamander shit) family becomes very important. Mind you, Heldanarr Fall is in short supply of that too. All of his other siblings and his father were killed years ago by Beasts of Chaos, and his mother (allegedly) ascended into the ranks of Sigmar’s Stormcast Eternals. All Fall has left in the world is his sister.

Beasts of Chaos army for the Michigan GT. Credit: Michael O "Muggins"

It is a grim existence, the forces of Chaos assaulting on one side and Azyrite exploitation on the other. Fall is trapped in the pressure cooker of circumstance; heated by the trauma of loss and the indignancy of injustice, as well as by the ambient fury of Aqshy, it is no wonder that he eventually embarks upon the most iconic of Warhammer of journeys… the Path to Glory.

This may be the best Path to Glory novel I have read, an in-depth and expansive exploration of the champion’s journey to corruption and victory. It details a journey that is more than just ‘I want more power so I’m going to devote myself to the dark gods, get myself a crab arm or whatever, and then go kill some good guys.’  Fall’s fall to the dark side is nuanced, tragic and, above all, deeply human.

He is a fascinating character with strong principles and values. But like anyone hoping to forge a path according to their conscience, he has to constantly reevaluate and recalibrate his ethics to fit the twisted reality in which he finds himself. He is highly driven, justice seeking, at times unflinchingly uncompromising, whilst at other times strangely compassionate. At some points in the book he is a bloodthirsty warlord, at other times an idealistic socialist revolutionary. He has a vision for his homeland where there is no exploitation or oppression, where there isn’t even currency, yet at the same time rivers literally run red with the blood he spills. The contradictions and dichotomies are rife, but such is the nature of the Path to Glory.

The Azyrites make for compelling villains in this story. Lady Lellen Se Roye is the viceroy-regent of Candip, Fall’s gentrified hometown. She is a greedy, corrupt and arrogant antagonist and her sister, the priestess Elene, is an entitled, elitist and effortlessly hate-able Sigmarite priestess. They are perfectly emblematic of Fall’s struggle, and are very effective at making you immediately want to fall into ranks behind him.  Even the city’s Stormcast Eternal Lord Imperatant, Ildrid Stormsworn of the Hammers of Sigmar, cannot stand the Se Royes and does everything she can do to halt their ambitions, doing her best to delay Candip's anointing as an official City of Sigmar.

Anyone who is fed up of getting shafted by their landlord, taken advantage of by their employer, or ripped off by wanky cafés, cannot help but have some sympathy for Fall. For a book set in a fantasy realm of fire, its themes are startlingly relatable.

But the forces of Order aren’t the only bad guys in this story. Chaos is an ever-present threat, and Fall knows this. Despite beginning to ally himself with he dark gods (while convincing himself he’s not), Fall will never forget that it was the Beastmen who were the ones who killed his family. Despite disappearing from the AOS game, they still serve as a really great reminder of the visceral, primal state of Chaos.  This makes for a great metaphor for what is going on within Fall, as he battles inwardly against the warping anger and compulsions within himself.

Blades of Khorne Blood Warriors. Credit: Rich Nutter

And then, of course, there is Khorne, the Blood God, the Godeater, constantly looking over Fall’s shoulder and inviting him to pledge himself to the dark gods and receive their boons; always seeking to corrupt his bloodlust and desire for martial greatness, vengeance and justice. Nguyen does a really great job of describing the wars on the battlefield, but he also portrays this battle for Fall’s soul really compellingly as well.

Naturally, following the Path to Glory will also bring you into contact with other warlords on their own intersecting paths.

Most prominent is Kaddarar the Seeker, a fully devoted follower of the Godeater.  She is a zealous and totally single-minded blade of Khorne.  And she’s also a bit sexy. Apparently. Turns out blood-crazed murder-barbarian is just the kind of woman Fall would swipe right for. As well as some hints of sexual tension between the two characters, you also have the tension that Kaddarar has promised to one day kill or be killed by Fall. As Chaos warps Fall’s notions of justice and fairness, so it also warps his notion of romance and love.

Boskin is also a really great character that Fall bumps into along the way.  He’s kind of portrayed as a bit of a lovable rogue, ducking and diving, not to be trusted, Del-Boy-esque. Motivated on the whole by greed, but not in a two-dimensional way, his Path is a fascinating one to watch unfold as Chaos warps his desires.

Yron is a mystic and devotee of the Chaos cult. Her path to glory is one that takes the course of rituals and rites.  She balances Fall’s determination not to have anything to do with any of the gods at all, and offers his followers faith where he rejects it. There is also Tominer, a Khornite priestess, who crops up from time to time and serves as an interesting vehicle for the book’s theology (another thing Nguyen does really well).

Jujjar is an old friend of Fall, well before he ever became the Godeater’s Son. He has a very different idea of where their movement should be going, and his own Path to Glory does not fit comfortably alongside Fall's, providing plenty of opportunity for narrative bumps along the way.

Indeed, Fall’s whole inner circle are a mishmash of diverse and antagonistic personalities, and it is his job to try to hold them all in tension, just as he has to unite the multitude of tribes, warbands and peoples that form his growing kingdom. Of course, none of this is quite as hard as the task Fall has of trying to hold together all of the disparate voices and desires within himself.

Even Fall’s horse, Micaw, an old clapped-out nag, is on her own Path to Glory of sorts.  Fall was originally planning to eat the horse at one point in the book, but he decides to spare her and use her for transportation instead. Now, with every unnatural mutation/boon the steed receives, shaping it more and more away from its original station as a beast of burden and towards its new form as a monstrous, reptilian, carnivorous war steed, we see a parallel with Fall’s own unnatural transformation.

What is actually really interesting about Fall is that he actually has a very hard time killing people once he gets to know them – which could be seen as a bit of deficiency in a warlord. Even his old nag was spared from becoming meat. This is a really fascinating dynamic in the book, and even becomes a key driving force in the sequel, Blood of the Godeater.

Ultimately, I’m not sure I have read such a thorough and interesting character study in an AOS novel. We all know the main thrust of Warhammer is often to say “there are no good guys, everyone’s a bit evil” but this book goes beyond that and says “here’s a human being, and he’s struggling with many of the things you, the reader, are struggling with, and actually he’s quite likeable sometimes, and identifiable, I think you might actually quite like him. Oh, but now he’s eating human flesh.”

All of this is coupled with the fact that Nguyen is really very good at putting words on a page, often slipping in little chunks of philosophy or observations about human behaviour that you don’t quite expect to find in a Warhammer book.

Garrek's Reavers. Credit: Magos Sockbert

There are some really good pieces of writing, and some delicious irony. Fall wears his father’s death mask throughout the book, all the time descending deeper towards the powers that claimed his father’s life. At the same time, Fall’s mother was rumoured to have been snatched up as a Stormcast Eternal, leaving behind the family she was supposedly trying to protect, exposing one of the greatest tragedies that religion can inflict upon a person; when a parent puts the love of their god ahead of the love of their own children. The result of this mother’s devotion to Order is that her son goes on to become a powerful Chaos warlord.

There’s one scene which is masterfully done, and I think symbolizes much of the whole book. Fall comes face to face with Ildrid Stormsworn, the Lord Imperitant, and they have a big fight. But while fighting they both try to get under each other’s skin and unravel the other mentally at the same time. They’re poking and prodding at each other’s psyche, trying to get the measure of the other – but they’re both doing so while hiding behind unexpressive masks. The book is richly layered, and makes the point very well that humans are too.

As far as world building goes, the book isn’t going to offer you a huge amount of general Age of Sigmar lore, it is mostly focused on the little corner of Aqshy in which it is set. There are some tidbits of Slaves to Darkness and Khorne lore, and a bit of Beasts of Chaos and Cities of Sigmar, but not a huge amount.

Urkhan the Dark Warden. Credit: Rich Nutter

However, the book really does build its own little narrative universe beautifully.  Strange mountains that lead to the Realm of Chaos, up-side-down cities hanging off the bottom of the world, ancient states and frontier towns, all trying to survive in the extreme heat of the Realm of Fire.  I really got a sense of place within the book, even if I did have to concentrate quite hard to remember all of the names and characteristics of the different tribes and peoples.

This book feels like a sweeping epic, but also like a detailed character piece. It tells the story of an empire being born, and of a soul being damned at the same time. Once you’ve read this book, you really know you’ve read it. Heldanarr Fall has stayed with me for a long time since I’ve finished. Ive thought about him a lot. I think this book is going to take its place as a classic Age of Sigmar book, and now I’m really looking forward to getting stuck into the sequel.

title: Games Workshop scraps Necromunda RPG a month after announcing it
content:
Games Workshop just dropped a bombshell. It will not be producing a Warhammer Necromunda tabletop RPG after all. The only explanation? "We've decided to focus our efforts on providing even more great minis for the core game". Oh… okay.

This has obviously caused quite a stir, and it must be said, is pretty odd. GW only announced Necromunda Roleplay a month ago, in a since-deleted Warhammer Community article published September 18. But you can't hide from the WayBackMachine, friends. We see you.

Necromunda Roleplay used a d100 system, and would've come with minis and prebuilt character sheets for an Escher Assassin, Orlock Gunslinger, Squat Fixer, or Goliath Champion PC - while also letting you build your own ganger from any of the six main Clan Houses. It was designed to be a mini-based RPG, compatible with the full Necromunda range, and with 18 minis included in the release box.

This wasn't just a far-off plan that GW decided not to go ahead with. They had lots of product shots ready, a very clear idea of what was in the core set box - right down to the rulebook page count - and promised a release date 'soon'. It seems likely this thing was ready to hit shelves before Christmas.

The sudden cancellation is a bolt from the blue, and speculation is rife, while hard facts are in short supply. People keep pointing to Cubicle 7, but in a Facebook post a few weeks ago, they said they've never had the Necromunda license. Truth is: we don't really know what happened here.

The cancellation will obviously be upsetting for tabletop RPG fans, but for those who really do just care about the minis, GW assures that those that were announced with Necromunda Roleplay will still be getting made. It's revealed a new roadmap for 2027 in fact. Here's that:

  • Spring 2027: Some Mad Max fun, a return to the Ash Wastes and WarCom teases "the biggest plastic vehicle kit yet" for Necromunda.
  • Summer 2027: Hive Secundus again, for grimy Malstrain Genestealer goodness.
  • Autumn 2027: 'Underhive Brutes' for the original six houses - teaser art shows a Luther pattern 'Ambot'
  • Winter 2027: Bounty hunters

Looks cool, but personally I'm way too distracted by the surprise cancellation just 35 days after the game was announced, to think much about that right now.

What happened? Share your wild theories with us over on the Wargamer Discord.

title: Lore Explainer: A Song of Ice and Fire - Fan Theories
content:
The story of A Song of Ice and Fire is notoriously sprawling and, painfully, still incomplete. “But keewa,” you might think “The TV show is finished; it is complete,” to which I would say, “Lies! The TV show is not canon! No! Get out of my house!”

Because the story is NOT FINISHED, the community of superfans online (I consider myself a superfan too) loves to come up with fan theories based on close readings of the text, the companion works and novellas, and general wild speculation. These theories range in importance from predicting how major plot details will shake out (if Winds ever gets finished) to completely inconsequential theories about complete ephemera.

As someone who has read an awful lot of these fan theories, allow me to share some of my favourites with you, whether because I think they’re likely to be accurate, they’re interesting, or just funny.

Note: This article will contain many spoilers for all books in A Song of Ice and Fire, I am going to assume that the reader is at least au fait with A Song of Ice and Fire and has read the main line of books as they currently stand and has an understanding of the story and its world; I’m not going to start out by explaining what Westeros is, put it that way.

Frey Pies

In A Dance With Dragons, Ramsay Bolton and “Arya Stark” (actually Jeyne Poole) are due to be married in Barrowton as the Northern army goes home after the War of Five Kings, and all the noble houses of the North are supposed to be represented in one way or another. The Boltons have a bit of a flair for the dramatic, and so they move the wedding to Winterfell, the castle they secretly sacked and burned after capturing Theon Greyjoy (and blaming the burning on him) all the way back in Book 2.

After the Red Wedding, three awful Freys are dispatched to White Harbour with the bones of Wyman Manderly’s son Wendel, both to return them to his home and to make sure Wyman remains loyal to the Iron Throne, presumably by reporting on him. The Iron Throne holds Wyman’s remaining son Wylis after his capture in the Riverlands. Wyman is a bit of a schemer himself, pretending to be a bluff and guileless fat guy, so he makes nice with the Freys until his living son is returned to him and everybody (including the Freys) set off to Winterfell for the wedding, even though the snow is falling pretty heavily. As they left White Harbour, Wyman gave the three Freys some nice horses as a guest gift, and at this point the Freys disappear from the story and don’t turn up again when the Manderlys arrive at Winterfell for the wedding with a lot of food for the celebration, including three huge wedding pies, described as

"three great wedding pies, as wide across as wagon wheels, their flaky crusts stuffed to bursting with carrots, onions, turnips, parsnips, mushrooms, and chunks of seasoned pork swimming in a savory brown gravy."

Wyman claims that he doesn’t know where the Freys got to, only that they got impatient with how slowly Wyman travels (since he can’t ride (too fat), he has to ride in a litter) and rode ahead on their horses.

Not a Frey Pie, but still, a very large pie.

The Frey Pies theory suggests (as you can probably guess from the name) that Wyman had the three Freys ambushed and murdered on the way to Winterfell and baked them into pies to serve to the Boltons and Freys in secret revenge for his son’s death at the Red Wedding.

There are lots of little textual hints that this theory is probably correct:

  • Wyman gives the three Freys fine horses as Guest Gifts when they depart White Harbour. The giving of Guest Gifts is seen as marking the end of the host’s obligation to their guests. Since the Red Wedding was a flagrant violation of Guest Right, waiting until after the giving of gifts to murder the Freys might be a symbol of Wyman wanting to do things “by the book” in contrast to the duplicitous actions of the Freys.
  • When Wyman secretly meets with Davos Seaworth, he tells him that he doesn’t believe the lies the Freys tell about the Red Wedding (Robb Stark started it by turning into a wolf and attacking the Freys, etc.), and expresses bitter anger towards them.

    “My son Wendel came to the Twins a guest. He ate Lord Walder's bread and salt, and hung his sword upon the wall to feast with friends. And they murdered him. Murdered, I say, and may the Freys choke upon their fables. I drink with Jared, jape with Symond, promise Rhaegar the hand of my own beloved granddaughter ... but never think that means I have forgotten. The north remembers, Lord Davos. The North remembers, and the mummer's farce is almost done. My son is home.” - Davos IV, ADWD.

  • Wyman serves the pies himself at the Wedding Feast, eagerly making sure that the prime culprits of the Red Wedding, the Freys and Boltons, eat pieces of the pies.
  • At the conclusion of the Winterfell wedding feast, a very drunk Wyman Manderly asks the singer to play a song about The Rat Cook. In an earlier book, Bran Stark reflects on the legend of the Rat Cook, a Night's Watchman who killed a visiting prince and served him to his father baked into a pie; the cook is then cursed by the gods by being turned into a monstrous rat. The story is explicit that the crime of the Rat Cook is not that of murder, but of breaching the custom of Guest Right by killing a guest beneath his roof (which Wyman accuses the Freys of doing).  
  • The pies are described as being filled with vegetables and pork - it’s said (by cannibals, presumably) that human meat tastes a lot like pork.

With all this evidence taken together, it’s pretty much certain that the three Freys were indeed baked into pies by Wyman Manderly.

Young Griff/Aegon Is Illyrio’s Son and a Blackfyre

Okay, this one is a little complicated, but please bear with me: there’s a lot to unpack. During A Dance with Dragons, Tyrion crosses paths with a party of adventurers in Essos when Illyrio places him with them; the leader of the group is a man called “Griff” travelling with his son “Young Griff”. If you’ve read ADWD, you know that Griff and Young Griff are actually Jon Connington and Aegon Targaryen, travelling incognito to meet Daenerys Targaryen. Aegon was allegedly spirited away by Varys from the Red Keep before his “murder” during the sack of King’s Landing, secreted across the Narrow Sea to Illyrio’s keeping so that one day he could reclaim the Iron Throne/Westeros.

It’s a pretty convenient story, so convenient that it’s hard to believe: let’s take a look at some evidence, shall we?

Daenerys has a bunch of trippy, prophetic visions in The House of the Undying in Qarth, while the Undying give her warnings, and a lot of the things shown in the House of the Undying are metaphorical and evocative predictions of things that do actually happen in the Story. Here’s the relevant passage:

“Glowing like sunset, a red sword was raised in the hand of a blue-eyed king who cast no shadow. A cloth dragon swayed on poles amidst a cheering crowd. From a smoking tower, a great stone beast took wing, breathing shadow fire. . . . mother of dragons, slayer of lies . . .”

Daenerys reflects on this with Jorah Mormont later in the same book:

““A mummer’s dragon, you said. What is a mummer’s dragon, pray?”

“A cloth dragon on poles,” Dany explained. “Mummers use them in their follies, to give the heroes something to fight.”

Ser Jorah frowned.”

 

Taken together, this vision implies that at some point in her story, Daenerys will encounter a fake dragon, a Mummer’s dragon, and that she will slay a “lie” related to it.

Three whole books later, Quaithe speaks to Daenerys through some mystical means, and reminds her (and us) about the Mummer’s Dragon once more:

"Hear me, Daenerys Targaryen. The glass candles are burning. Soon comes the pale mare, and after her the others. Kraken and dark flame, lion and griffin, the sun's son and the mummer's dragon. Trust none of them. Remember the Undying. Beware the perfumed seneschal." 

Who is this “Mummer’s dragon”? There’s really only one candidate - Young Griff, aka “Aegon Targaryen”. As the only other person in the story claiming to be a Targaryen, Young Griff is immediately suspicious; this suspicion is only reinforced by Young Griff’s association with Illyrio and Varys… Two very adept schemers. But wait! Wasn’t Varys a mummer before he was castrated and became a spymaster? Yes, yes he was! With this information in hand, we can quite confidently say that “Aegon” is the Mummer’s Dragon, and as such is almost certainly not a Targaryen. George RR Martin knows a lot of English history, and he knows very well that there have been several instances of royal pretenders claiming to be the lost Princes In The Tower, returned from exile overseas.

Well then who is he? That question is far less certain, but there is a relatively convincing theory that “Aegon” is actually a Blackfyre. The Blackfyres were a pseudo-cadet branch of House Targaryen founded by a legitimised bastard known as Daemon Blackfyre; they then fought several failed civil wars (known as Blackfyre Rebellions) against the Targaryens to try and take control of the throne. They typically share the classic Targaryen traits of blonde hair and purple eyes, too. The Blackfyres were finally wiped out some thirty years before the main story begins, when Barristan Selmy killed Maelys the Monstrous, the final male Blackfyre.  But wait, “Aegon” is only 16 years old; if the last Blackfyre died thirty years ago, how can he possibly be a Blackfyre? Well, Maelys was the last male Blackfyre; it’s entirely possible that the Blackfyre family continued through the female line. If so, it’s possible that “Aegon’s” mother was a Blackfyre, living incognito in Essos.

There’s a fun bit of imagery that hints towards this in A Feast For Crows: The Inn at the Crossroads once had a black dragon sign made of wrought iron, but following the first rebellion, the local lord was angered by the sight of it, cut the sign to pieces, and threw it in the river. Some years later, one of the dragon’s heads washed up on a tidal island known as the Quiet Isle, but in the intervening time it had become red with rust. A black dragon that goes to the sea and returns to Westeros coloured red (on the outside).

Illyrio Mopatis’ second wife was called Serra - he shares his story with Tyrion in ADWD. To give a short précis: He met her in a brothel in Lys and liked her so much he brought her home, at some undetermined point later, she got greyscale and died. Illyrio keeps her turned-to-stone hands and wears a locket with her portrait in it, which he shows to Tyrion. Serra is described as having blue eyes and blonde hair streaked with silver, typically Valyrian traits, though this might not mean much since Lyseni tend to share Valyrian traits more than the other peoples of the world. This extension of the Blackfyre theory suggests that Illyrio’s wife Serra was, in fact, Serra Blackfyre, and that Illyrio intends to get “Aegon” on the throne to fulfil some kind of promise to the wife he loved so much that he keeps her hands in his bedroom.

But wait, there’s more! Some fans take this theory even farther to suggest that Varys himself is also a Blackfyre, potentially even the sibling of Serra. This is a bit “out there” - some fans believe the reason Varys was sold as a slave, castrated, and his penis used in a magic ritual by a sorcerer is that he also possesses King’s Blood, through his Blackfyre ancestry, and King’s Blood is noted throughout the series by magic users as being a kind of catalyst that makes magic spells more powerful (Melisandre relies on this quite a few times in the novels).

Adherents of this particular extended theory claim that Varys isn’t actually bald, but shaves his head to disguise his silver-blonde Valyrian hair. The relevant evidence put forth for this is that, when introduced, Varys is described as being “as hairless as an egg”. In the Dunk and Egg novellas, Aegon Targaryen (Egg) shaves his head to disguise his silver-blonde Valyrian hair.

Obviously, the implications of “Aegon” being both a pretender and a Blackfyre would have huge implications for the wider story of A Song of Ice and Fire, so if this one is true, it’ll be pretty seismic.

Peter Claffey as Dunk in A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms: Copyright HBO

Hodor Is Dunk’s Great Grandson/Dunk Had Sex with Old Nan

In Bran’s final chapter in A Dance With Dragons, he continues his greenseer training with Bloodraven, looking into the past through the eyes of Winterfell’s Heart Tree. Later, when going to sleep, he has a dream composed of a bunch of visions from the same Heart Tree in quick succession, going backwards in time – one of these visions is as follows:

“Then there came a brown-haired girl slender as a spear who stood on the tips of her toes to kiss the lips of a young knight as tall as Hodor.”

There are a bunch of textual hints as to the implications of this single sentence.

  • The scene takes place in Winterfell, and we know that Old Nan has always lived in Winterfell. Dunk and Egg visited Winterfell at some point between The Mystery Knight and Egg’s coming of age. Old Nan would be a similar age to Dunk, if he were still alive.
  • Hodor is explicitly mentioned as a comparison, and Old Nan is Hodor’s great-grandmother. Hodor is unusually tall and strong, standing over 7 feet - Dunk is also around 7 feet tall.
  • The man is described as a knight - knighthood is unusual in the North, since they do not follow the Faith of the Seven, which is the religious grouping in Westeros that has knighthood. Dunk is, of course, a knight.
  • Another especially tall and strong character has been confirmed by GRRM to be a descendant of Dunk - Brienne. 

As to how this affects the story, well, I can’t think of any way that Hodor’s parentage would have much impact on the plot, but even so, it’s a nice little potential wink towards the Dunk and Egg stories in the main series.

Tywin Lannister Secret Sex Tunnel/Marei

During the events of A Clash of Kings, Tyrion visits a fancy, high-class brothel in King’s Landing called Chataya’s as a cover for secretly paying visits to his lover Shae. This deception involves entering the brothel, ostensibly as a customer, going to the fanciest room in the place, where he is met by Varys, who opens a secret passage and accompanies him to a stable. While they do so, Varys provides some information about the provenance of this secret passage.

“How is it a brothel happens to have a secret entrance?”

“The tunnel was dug for another King’s Hand, whose honor would not allow him to enter such a house openly. Chataya has closely guarded the knowledge of its existence.”

 

Who is a good candidate for this Hand of the King who maintains a severe and honourable public persona, but visits the city’s most expensive brothel on the sly? The earlier part of the chapter provides some sneaky little clues as to his identity.

“Over the door swung an ornate lamp, a globe of gilded metal and scarlet glass.”

“Within the room was a great canopied bed, a tall wardrobe decorated with erotic carvings, and a narrow window of leaded glass in a pattern of red and yellow diamonds.”

Taken together, these conspicuous descriptions of decorations in red and gold, including the window of the fancy sex room itself, suggest that the randy Hand is, in fact, Lord Tywin Lannister himself. He who chides Tyrion for using the services of sex workers and is claimed to have not even touched a woman since his beloved wife died is a massive hypocrite, revealed fully when he has sex with Shae herself shortly before being killed by Tyrion.

But that’s not all! One of the workers in the brothel is a girl called Marei, who is described as being pale, solemn, and having blonde hair and green eyes. Blonde hair and green eyes are classic Lannister traits, so building on the suggestion of Tywin’s sex tunnel, it’s possible to imagine that Marei is actually Tywin Lannister’s bastard daughter. Marei is older than Shae, who is 18 during the events of Game of Thrones, placing her birth year at 281 AC - meaning Marei was probably born either in 280AC or before. When was Tywin Lannister the Hand of the King? From 262 until 281AC.

The dates match up pretty cleanly, so it’s entirely possible that Marei really is Tywin’s bastard daughter; and therefore a half-sister to Cersei, Jaime, and Tyrion. It’s a good thing she didn’t sleep with Tyrion!

What impact does any of this have on the story? None whatsoever; it’s just more easter-egg evidence that Tywin Lannister was a massive hypocrite.

Sam Tarly Has the Horn of Winter

During A Clash of Kings, Ghost leads Jon Snow - potentially via some Old Gods magic - to a cache of Dragonglass blades and arrowheads, wrapped up in a Night’s Watch cloak and buried at the Fist of the First Men. Also present in this cache is a cracked old war horn, which he gives to Sam Tarly because, as a book-learnin’ kind of guy, he figures that Sam will like a useless artefact.

At around the same time, the wildlings, led by Mance Rayder, are searching ancient graves for a powerful magic artefact called the Horn of Joramun, or the Horn of Winter – a legendary horn with the power to destroy The Wall once sounded. Mance plans to use this horn as a bargaining chip in order to force the Night's Watch to let the Wildlings through The Wall so they can shelter behind it, since the Others can’t pass through the magic wards built into The Wall. It’s a pretty desperate gambit. Threatening the Night's Watch to either let them through the Wall or they’ll destroy it altogether and doom everybody is quite high-stakes, to put it mildly. Mance claims to have found the Horn of Winter and brings it with him when the Wildlings march on The Wall. After their surprise defeat by the forces of Stannis Baratheon, both Mance Rayder and the Horn are captured, and the Horn is ritually burned by Melisandre. However, in the time between the Wildling’s capture and Jon Snow’s murder, he is told several times by friendly Wildlings that the Horn was never found, and the one burned by Melisandre was a fake, intended to bluff the Night’s Watch.

“Melisandre burned the Horn of Joramun.”

“Did she?” Tormund slapped his thigh and hooted. “She burned that fine big horn, aye. A bloody sin, I call it. A thousand years old, that was. We found it in a giant’s grave, and no man o’ us had ever seen a horn so big. That must have been why Mance got the notion to tell you it were Joramun’s. He wanted you crows to think he had it in his power to blow your bloody Wall down about your knees. But we never found the true horn, not for all our digging. If we had, every kneeler in your Seven Kingdoms would have chunks o’ ice to cool his wine all summer.”

Jon XII - A Dance With Dragons

 

So, if we accept that the Horn of Winter is real, and that it has already appeared in the narrative (admittedly a big leap), there’s only one candidate as to which horn it can be - the cracked Warhorn Jon mysteriously found on the Fist of the First Men, which he subsequently passed on to Samwell Tarly. Maybe a Night's Watchman ranger found the horn in the wild, and realising its true nature, took it to the Fist and buried it surrounded with blades of dragonglass, to prevent the Others from getting hold of it. The horn is mentioned a bunch of times, too many times for it to simply be an unimportant bit of junk. When Sam left The Wall, he took the horn with him to Oldtown, so it’s currently about as far from The Wall as it’s possible to be while still being in Westeros, so it’s safely out of the way, right?

Well… Euron Greyjoy - who has recently displayed some troublingly apocalyptic desires of his own - is currently attacking the Reach and threatening Oldtown itself. Were he to acquire this potential Horn of Winter, the existential situation Westeros faces would quickly go from bad to worse.

Rory McCann as The Hound in HBO's Game of Thrones - Credit: HBO

The UnKiss

During the Battle of the Blackwater in A Clash of Kings, Sandor Clegane, traumatised by the massive conflagration of burning ships, deserts his position, gets extremely drunk, and plans to leave the city.  On his way out the door, he visits Sansa Stark’s bedchamber and, in a very uncomfortable passage, offers to take her with him. When she declines, he threatens her with a knife and demands she sing a song for him. After she finishes singing, he rips off his bloodstained white cloak and leaves.

What’s more peculiar about this scene comes later: Sansa reflects on this event several times as her story progresses, mostly when the topic hinges around intimacy or kissing, but something about her recollection is amiss - each time she thinks about the night of the Blackwater, Sansa remembers The Hound kissing her, although this didn’t happen.

“Sansa wondered what Megga would think about kissing the Hound, as she had. He’d come to her the night of the battle stinking of wine and blood. He kissed me and threatened to kill me, and made me sing him a song.”

- A Storm of Swords, Sansa II

“As the boy’s lips touched her own she found herself thinking of another kiss. She could still remember how it felt, when his cruel mouth pressed down on her own. He had come to Sansa in the darkness as green fire filled the sky. He took a song and a kiss, and left me nothing but a bloody cloak.”

- A Feast For Crows “Alayne” II

Later in the same chapter, Sansa is asked if she knows what goes on in a marriage bed:

“She thought of Tyrion, and of the Hound and how he’d kissed her, and gave a nod”.

So why does Sansa remember kissing The Hound when that clearly did not happen? Search me, I have no idea. GRRM has, however, said that Sansa’s faulty memory of this event will be important later in the story, so this oddity still warrants a mention.

Sansa and the Ashford Tourney Champions

Another oddity in Sansa’s story has been remarked upon by fans since A Feast For Crows came out… oh my god, 21 years ago. In AFFC, Petyr Baelish organises a betrothal between Sansa (in her guise as his bastard daughter Alayne) and Harrold Hardyng, the heir apparent of the sickly Robert Arryn. Eagle-eyed readers recalled a detail from The Hedge Knight, the first Dunk and Egg novella from 1998 - in The Hedge Knight, the final roster of champions for Lady Ashford’s birthday tournament is:

  • Lyonel Baratheon
  • Leo Tyrell
  • Tybolt Lannister
  • Humfrey Hardyng
  • Valarr Targaryen

Sansa was first betrothed to Joffrey Baratheon before he cast her aside for Margaery Tyrell. After being cast aside by Joffrey, Olenna Tyrell suggests marrying her to Willas Tyrell. This marriage plan reaches the ears of the Lannisters, who interrupt it by forcibly marrying Sansa to Tyrion Lannister. After the Purple Wedding, Tyrion’s capture, and Sansa’s flight with Littlefinger, he attempts to marry her to Harrold Hardyng. If this pattern holds true, it implies that Sansa will marry, or be promised to marry, someone from House Targaryen.

You could argue “but they’re all great houses; it makes sense that Sansa Stark might get betrothed to any one of them”, but the inclusion of House Hardyng casts a spanner in this line of thinking, because, in the grand scheme of things, the Hardyngs are a nothing-family; they’re not even nobility, just landed knights. If Harold weren’t, by a series of very unlikely familial ties, the heir to the Eyrie, he’d never be considered a match for someone as important as Sansa Stark. GRRM loves leaving little hints in his work, and the coincidence is too strange to be discounted out of hand.

That's my roundup and explanation of only a few of the very, very many fan theories bouncing around the A Song of Ice and Fire fan community. What do you think? Are any of them likely to be accurate? Let me know on the Discord!

title: BattleTechnical: GM Force Building Walkthrough
content:
In this third part of our mini-series on building campaign OpFors, I’m going to work through my process as I put together the force I’m going to run in a campaign game. In part one, I took a look at what kind of information I wanted to have ready as I started building my force and got a general sense of how I want my forces equipped. In part two I looked at the different types of mechs I’m going to fill most of my force with, along with specific examples of those mechs. Here we’re going to put it all together – I have a mission and a player force, and I’m going to walk through most of my thoughts as I get this campaign game set up.

The Mission

As presented to the players, this mission has a convoy moving prisoners through a city. They need to engage the escorts while friendly units rescue the prisoners. However, I want to flip this mission around a little bit and it’s actually going to be an ambush – this is the third prison break mission in a row the players have been doing as part of a contract, and I think the government has gotten wind of what’s going on. Having an ambush also provides me a perfect opportunity to tweak forces on the fly depending on exactly how well the players are doing with the escorts – if they kill the escorts quickly without taking much damage I bring the full ambush force in, but if Murphy shows up and the players somehow get too beat up I can immediately scale the ambushers back. I’m going to make the actual objective be escaping off the board, and to give them a little bit of extra spice I’m going to need them to have eight hexes between their units and any of the OpFor units when they move off the board.

In this contract the players are fighting the Isle of Skye in 3152, so I’m building forces that are primarily a mix of Republic and Lyran mechs, with a scattering of Wolf Empire and Jade Falcon salvage if I need it. With no current MUL faction list for the Isle of Skye this is my best guess for what kind of government forces would be found.

Sword of Light Rokurokubi. Credit: Jack Hunter

The Player Forces

I’ve got eight players in this campaign, and I require them to tell me which of their mechs they’re running in each mission a few days before the actual game. We have quite a bit of customization going on, and for this mission they’re fielding two Rokurokubi’s, a Venom, an Ostsol, a Lament, a Jade Hawk, a Stormwolf, and a Warhammer. Many of these are custom so I need to go dig into their record sheets to see exactly what they can do, but even at a glance there are a few things I can immediately figure out:

  • The Stormwolf is significantly over-BVed for its firepower. I can’t count on it actually contributing 3200 BV of value.
  • Their slowest mech moves 4/6. Since I’m requiring them to put some distance between themselves and the ambushers I’m going to want to make sure I don’t run too many 5/8 ambushers, and trigger the ambush in a way that gives them an escape route. I’m avoiding the 5/8s because that tends to be a spot where mechs keep a lot of durability alongside their speed – at 6/9 they start becoming a lot more fragile (though I also don’t want to swarm them with too many fast mechs either). It also informs me some on map setup/deployment – we typically get 10 turns in, so the Warhammer will get no more than 60 MP. If I want to trigger the ambush somewhere around turn 3, that would give it 42 MP to extract with. Including some MP for turning and not wanting to run in a completely straight line, I want to make sure that the Warhammer is around 25-30 hexes from the table edge it extracts on when the ambush happens.
  • With three lights their overall firepower isn’t going to be amazing. It’s not going to be terrible, because I know the refits increase damage significantly, but I don’t want to just throw a pile of assault mechs at them.

Next I’m going to actually look at their record sheets. I can see that with their pilot skills they have about 20k BV, so in a normal game if I threw about 19k at them all at once (slightly lower to account for the Stormwolf) I’d expect them to win with a couple casualties. I already know my forces will be split into escorts and ambushers, and that I want the players to need to flee, so assuming that my escorts are fairly weak I’m going to want somewhere a bit over 20k in the ambush force. When I look at their mechs, I get a couple extra bits of info:

  • Many of them have active probes. I fortunately didn’t see any bloodhounds, but they have a couple beagles with 4-hex range and one watchdog with 5-hex range. When I’m deploying the ambushers I’ll need to keep them out of that range, which will help me with keeping an escape route open. It’ll also weaken any super short range ambushers I field, since they won’t be able to start quite at point blank.
  • The Venom has a lot more gun damage than I expected, while the Ostsol has less as it’s been built for TSM.
  • Their only 15-point hits are on the Lament, so I’m not worried over much about having mechs getting taken out by headshots.

The OpFor

Between the mission and the player units I’ve now got a good sense of what I need. A pretty cheap escort force that I can expect the players to chew up in just a couple turns, and about 20k BV of ambushers. The escort force will be especially good if I can use it to get the players strung out a bit with their slow mechs closer to their escape route.

Titan Tactical Brigade Starslayer. Credit: Jack Hunter

The Escorts

This is the easy part to start with. I just finished painting a lance of mostly shitboxes, so I’m going to grab variants of these that seem likely to be used as bait. I’m mostly concerned with not being able to do too much damage and dying quickly, which these should be great at.

Starslayer STY-3C

The only actually good mech in this force, the Starslayer is still just a medium with moderate damage. I wish it had an XL, but even with a standard engine it shouldn’t be hard to kill.

Assassin ASN-30

It’s a medium laser and an LBX AC/5. It really doesn’t do much, even if I shoot light mechs with it. With only one ton of ammo I’m going to only run slug, both to keep the game fast and to cut down on chances of a random cockpit hit.

Vulcan VT-5Sr

I’ve got a choice between the 5Sr and 7T here, and since I want this lance to be bad I’m taking the 5Sr. Less armor and a lack of a targeting computer is exactly what I want when my goal is accomplishing little.

Scorpion SCP-1TB

Again I’m going for the worst of the available variants. Low armor and low damage is exactly what I’m looking for.

All told, these four mechs should die very quickly, being unable to build up too much TMM or having a lot of armor. If the non-Starslayers can all die in the first 2-3 turns I’ll be happy.

Hastati Sentinels Highlander. Credit: Jack Hunter

The Ambushers

I’m looking about eight units in my ambush force. I don’t want too many, because that’s  going to slow gameplay down too far, but having too few means that I’m risking some lucky hits not creating the mission outcome I’m intending (yes, this is somewhat on rails; this is a BattleTech campaign not Dungeons & Dragons). I’m going to want one mech that’s slow, short ranged, and threatening – this is something that forces them to run away. I’ll add a couple of killable heavy or assault units at 4/6 movement, which will keep up with the players and force them to commit to some fighting rather than purely fleeing, and pad out with some faster mediums that the light mechs can tangle with.

Highlander HGN-734

I started off looking for a 3/5 assault with some variety of AC 20. This is definitely killable by the players with a light engine and a bunch of ammo in one torso, but it’s durable enough that I think they’ll try to avoid it rather than killing it. A large laser means it doesn’t do nothing at range, but it doesn’t do much – it’s mostly there to terrify the players and make them flee.

Doloire DLR-OA

This is definitely a good mech, though it’s not quite 100% armor coverage and has a light engine to keep it reasonable to kill. I picked a variant that doesn’t hit for more than 10 damage with any single shot and doesn’t have any accuracy bonuses beyond the AES – I want a threat, not to immediately kill the players.

Marauder MAD-5S

An XL engine marauder is an easy choice as a killable threat. It’s not one of the variants that maxes out armor, so it’s a good place for our only long range 15-damage weapon.

Thunderbolt TDR-11SE

Another good mech that doesn’t hit tremendously hard, I grabbed this because it brings ECM, 6 jump is useful in a city, and it has extremely bad heat efficiency. It’s a decent threat, but probably won’t be killing anything.

Axman AXM-3Sr

The last of our heavies, this is another less-than-fully armored 4/6 heavy. It doesn’t have any big hits, will hopefully sandblast the players down without killing them, and is something they can kill. Another ECM makes me narratively happy.

Hunchback HBK-7R

This is one where I’m not entirely sure how it’ll end up playing. It carries an ultra ac/10, which can be swingy, and has reinforced structure. In some ways its more durable than the heavy mechs, although an XL engine does keep it honest.

Bushwacker BSW-X2

I love Bushwackers, I’m playing a Lyran-ish force, they’re easy to kill, and this one’s a bit of a mess of capabilities. Easy include.

Griffin IIC 7

This picks up some mobility that I wanted but the rest of the force lacks and a little bit of an accuracy improvement to threaten the light mechs, but ER pulses mean its not enough to reliably kill them. It’ll be a useful skirmisher to try to keep everything moving.

Firestarter Omni FS9-OE

One mech more than I really wanted to include, but I wasn’t quite at the power level I wanted (especially knowing the Highlander will probably only be minimally involved in fighting). This brings in one more quick medium, an MRM 20 is enough damage to be a real threat, and it has a sword, which is bad but funny.

In theory, this force should be enough to make sure the players don’t have the option to stick around and just kill it, even if they get some good luck, but because I’ve piled a lot of the threat into slower short ranged mechs it won’t be able to just wipe them off the map. The ambush force entirely runs light and XL engines, so are fragile enough that they should start dropping quickly, but will last long enough to push the players off the map. I’m most concerned with my requirement that successful extraction has no mechs within 8 hexes – it shouldn’t be a problem for the fast units, but might be an issue for the Warhammer.

The Game

On the table, this force ended up working out close to how I was planning. I didn’t quite anticipate the player actions right, and they triggered the ambush earlier than expected – the escort units weren’t dead, and the Venom was dead center in the middle of the ambush, forcing me to split fire so as to not instantly evaporate it on turn 2. I had expected them to play a little cagier, trying to take out the escorts before capturing the transports, but they sprinted straight in (the transports wouldn’t have escaped until about turn 5, so they had plenty of time).

I didn’t quite succeed at forcing the players to focus fire and take out the heavier units. My 4/6s were never quite able to catch up to their Warhammer, so the players only truly had to contend with the lighter units – things that even part of their force at a time were able to take out. This tends to be an issue with these larger campaign games, as players are very worried about losing their mechs and will prioritize playing safe over killing things, but large games have too much damage on the field, such that exposing mechs dramatically increases risk of loss. There unfortunately isn’t a great solution to that – for a campaign situation where you want mechs to survive, playing games at closer to 10k BV than 20k BV (which generally means having 4 players instead of 8) is just much more functional.

In hindsight, I think swapping one of the heavies (probably the Axman) for another 5/8 or 6/9 unit would’ve given me a game a little closer to what I wanted. I think having one more unit that could keep up with and pressure the players would’ve forced them to stick around and fight more, but it also might’ve just led to them abandoning the Warhammer and having their other units escape – hard to know for sure in advance. That brings me to my last thought (at least for now) on building these forces: know your players. This mission could’ve gone very differently if the players played differently, and I probably should’ve expected them to slam something forward and trigger the ambush ASAP, despite how cagey they tend to play once they get into actual combat.

title: Greenwood is a huge hit at Essen Spiel, but is this new board game worth the hype?
content:
On opening day of Essen Spiel, board game fans queued around corners to get a glimpse of Greenwood. The rebellious fantasy strategy title has been hyped to high heaven online, and boy, did gamers show up to see what the fuss was about. I sat down for one of the new game's first demos to see if the hype was deserved.

What first grabbed me was the theme. Greenwood is, on the surface, a quaint fantasy game where you ramble the titular forests, taking in nature and cavorting with cutesy creatures. In reality, it's a guerilla act of sabotage. The adorable inhabitants of Greenwood are held there against their will, and you're here to rescue them.

Like all great strategy games, Greenwood is a cluster of interconnected engines. They seem imposing at first glance, but you fall into rhythm very quickly.

Each round begins at Dusk, when you choose three of four possible perks: play a companion card onto your board, place a protection token on a threat card, discard a card to move up the Aurora track, and/or increase your Strength.

Already, I've thrown a lot of concepts at you. Let's break them down.

Your hand of cards represents many things. When played onto your board, they are allies who can aid you with unique abilities. To activate said powers, you'll place an Energy token on the card during the Night phase. You also have Spy tokens that copy the power of opponents' companions, but generally, it's one token per card. The same goes for Hiking tokens, which are placed on your cards to take a Move/Map action rather than activate their ability.

Now, onto Protection tokens. The Druids who rule Greenwood become increasingly suspicious of your sabotage as the nights go on. This is represented by a Threat track, which gains more cards with each round. Threat cards offer penalties when placing your Spy token, but Protection tokens negate this - and get you a nice extra bonus to boot.

Next, let's talk about the tracks. Strength represents your physical might. It grants various bonuses as you ascend, and it opens additional slots for Knowledge tokens. You collect these via a Study action and by discarding cards to gather your desired tokens. More on these tokens later.

Similar to Strength, the main board has a Wayfinder track that offers bonuses for investing in it. This might be anything from points to cards to Energy tokens. Basically, these are your two 'engine-building' tracks, designed to unlock additional, more powerful turns. You can up your Wayfinder track in all sorts of ways, from visiting specific places on the map to improving your other tracks.

The last track to track (somebody stop me) is your Aurora. After a simultaneous Dusk phase, everyone takes Departure actions equal to their Aurora value. That might mean removing Hiking tokens from cards or using specific powers called Spells. There's some base Spells available to everyone, but companions often offer more.

After that, Night falls, and the rescue mission begins. You'll take turns placing a Hiking token, Energy, or Spy on companions until you choose or have to pass.

So far, Greenwood sounds like a game of pushing tracks as high as they go. It sort of is, but there's a point to it that makes this more than just a spreadsheet.

The ultimate goal is to rescue those aforementioned cuddly critters. You'll collect and discard their matching Knowledge tokens, move to their space on the map, and sweep them to the safety of your personal submarine. Suddenly, your refugees are transformed into tetrominoes. These must be carefully slotted into your cramped sub, with placement rewards for filling columns and slots. It's very Feast for Odin, though Greenwood is nowhere near as complex.

Perhaps that easy comparison is, for me, the difference between 'liking' and 'loving' Greenwood. It's impressive how seamless everything feels, don't get me wrong. Greenwood is a well-oiled strategic machine that glides as smooth as a stealthy submarine. It manages to be challenging without off-putting. For all it's decision points, turns move quickly, with very little to trip you up and gum its gears.

But it's nothing we haven't seen before. Perhaps a full game - or several - would reveal to me Greenwood's idiosyncrasies. I can only give my first impression: a strategy game whose tried-and-tested mechanics work flawlessly, but feel rather too safe.

I have my issues too with the theme, the very thing that drew me to Greenwood in the first place. It's unique and well-realized by the game's lovely art and production. However, I don't fully understand why a covert rescue mission is a competitive endeavor.

Surely, as vigilantes with a shared goal, we'd want to work together? Why are we spying on each other and quibbling over who gets to be the 'best' rescuer? Greenwood presents a thrilling story about a fight for freedom, but it never really commits to telling that story with its mechanics.

I'd love to play Greenwood again. There's an engaging engine here worth exploring. But, for me, it wasn't an instant buy.

Want to learn more about Essen's best games? Check out our coverage from the show floor, posted in the Wargamer Discord. Or, check out our best board games guide for this year's top titles.

title: [40k] Ruleshammer 11th Edition: Article Updates #4 with Orks Q&A
content:
Welcome back to Ruleshammer! In this series we take a detailed look at the rules of key games, but Warhammer 40k in particular. This week I’m covering a few of your questions you’ve submitted via the Ruleshammer form or via Discord.

Cover and Visibility Q&A

How does cover work when some INFANTRY models are fully visible but within a terrain area, and some models are not fully visible but not within a terrain area?

The key thing to remember in these scenarios is that the cover penalty applies to attacking models and is checked per attacking model when declaring targets; this means you can have some situations where some models in a unit have the penalty apply, and some don’t. This particular scenario, though, is better explained with the diagram below.

For more guides and Q&A on cover and visibility rules check out my Terrain Guide.

Orks Q&A

Riled Up Questions

Ork Boyz Part 2. Credit: Kevin Stillman

If a unit makes an advance move and then gets riled up, can that unit declare charge?

While a unit is riled up:

      • <some other abilities>
      • When that unit is selected to make an advance move, that advance move does not prevent that unit from being eligible to declare a charge.

No. Specifically the unit needs to be riled up because this effect only causes advance moves made whilst riled up to not prevent a unit from being eligible to declare a charge. The important element is that it’s “that advance move” made “while riled up” that has this benefit. It’s not a blanket “riled up units can charge even if they advanced this turn” ability.

Can a Warboss use the Intimidating Motivation ability to rile up himself and advance and charge?

Warboss. Credit: Rockfish

Intimidating Motivation (Once per battle round, per army): In your Movement phase, at the start or end of this unit’s move, you can select one friendly ORKS unit within 6" of this unit. That unit:

    • Is no longer battle-shocked.
    • Is riled up until the start of your next turn.

Yes. Though, wow is this wording a bit tricky here. The ability is very much geared towards the Warboss being able to select another unit either within 6” of where it is now or within 6” of a position it has moved to. However the unit is definitely within 6” of itself and it’s a friendly Orks unit, so it can be used on itself.

The other question though is if “starts its move” is the same timing as “when selected to make an advance move.” The consensus here at Tabletop Battles was yes, that “starts its move” is the moment a unit is selected to move next and therefore the unit was riled up at the time it was selected to make an advance move. So the unit is riled up when selecting the advance move and that advance move wouldn’t prevent the unit from advancing and charging.

Can a Warboss use the Intimidating Motivation ability if they remain stationary?

No. Despite being a "move type" the effect of Remain Stationary means it doesn't allow this ability to be triggered.

EFFECT: No models are moved (either in straight lines or rotated). Units that remain stationary do not trigger any rules that are triggered when a unit starts or ends a move.

Which does mean that a Warboss in combat that doesn't fall back can't use this ability to rile up their unit or another nearby unit.

If I do Tactical Disembark with my Warboss unit, can I use his Intimidating Motivation ability before he makes an Advance move and Charge on the same turn?

Yes. For the same reasoning as the other question though with some Transport flavour thrown in. First of all the ability would be used at the start of the move, which in this case is when you declare the unit is disembarking. Some players at this point might ask a few questions such as “does the ability work when the unit isn’t on the battlefield?” Yes it does.

Q: Do a unit's abilities continue to function while they are embarked within a TRANSPORT?

A: Yes, within the restrictions specified by the ability itself. Embarked units are Not On The Battlefield (01.02.04), so any ability requiring visibility or measurement to another unit will fail.

Some might then say, “But this ability requires measurement, so does that prevent it from working?” No, it does not, because of the rule mentioned in that FAQ answer:

01.02.04 Not On The Battlefield

    • …
    • Players cannot measure distances to or from that unit (units are within range of their own abilities).

So a unit's abilities still function and the unit is in range of its own abilities even while embarked. So we can declare it is being used as the Disembark begins, and it will be riled up before it advances, allowing it to charge later on in that turn.

Note you can’t actually select it after disembarking but before advancing though despite this ability being usable at the end of a move. This is because Tactical Disembark doesn’t end until the Advance move has been made based on the rules for moving units.

Ending a Move

After you have finished setting up all of the models in a unit and/or moving all of the models in a unit that you want to move, check that all of the following apply:

    • If that unit is on the battlefield, it is in coherency (03.03).
    • No models in that unit are on another model or partway through a surface of a terrain feature (e.g. a wall or ceiling).
    • All stated ‘After Moving’ conditions are met.

The advance move is an after moving condition of the Tactical Disembark move, and I’m not sure we can argue it’s been met until that advance move has been completed.

Can the Grab It Stratagem be used to embark a unit into a Trukk?

Credit: Contemptor Kevin Stillman

Yes, with some limitations. The Grab It stratagem requires a unit to end its move within range of an objective:

Which it will do, but that condition only applies to the end of the Normal move. It doesn’t need to end the turn within range of the objective, just the move. Units need to meet certain conditions to embark though:

Once the first battle round has started, a friendly unit can embark within a friendly TRANSPORT model after making a normal, advance or fall-back move, if all of the following conditions apply:

    • Each model in that unit is within 3" of that TRANSPORT.
    • That unit was not set up on the battlefield this turn.
    • That unit is eligible to embark within that TRANSPORT, as described on that TRANSPORT’s datasheet.
    • That TRANSPORT has sufficient remaining transport capacity for each model in that unit.

Some are obvious, like the Transport needs to have capacity for them to embark. Some are more subtle, though, such as this combination of rules not working if the unit targeted with the Grab It Stratagem was set up on the battlefield this turn, either by having disembarked or arrived from reserves.

Can a Weirdboy leading a Beast Snagga Boyz unit embark within a Kill Rig?

Ork Kill Rig. Credit: Magos Sockbert

No. Whilst the unit would have the BEAST SNAGGA BOYZ keyword, the required keyword to embark within a Kill Rig the Weirdboy model itself would not gain this keyword from leading the unit.

19.03 Keywords in Attached Units

An attached unit has all of the keywords of all of its component units. As such, an attached unit is affected by any rule that applies to units with any of those keywords. Note that models in an attached unit do not gain the keywords of other models in that unit that they do not already have. Remember that attacks target units, not models.

Transport capacities are checking model keywords not unit keywords.

These questions and answers will be added to Ruleshammer 11th Edition: Orks.

That's all for this weeks Ruleshammer; if you have some questions you think I should cover in the future though please do send them via this form!
