title: Trench Crusade Faction Focus: The Court of the Seven-Headed Serpent (Updated October 23, 2026)
content:
Today we’re back with our weekly Trench Crusade article, and this time, it seems that we’re not quite done with Hell just yet. In what can be described as Divine serendipity, since we recently covered the Sins of the Court, Factory Fortress Inc. released its latest October update, which focuses on Hell's denizens. 

Changelog

  • Update (Latest): 2026-10-23 Updated to reflect changes to the faction in the October update.
  • Published: 2026-1-30

The Lore

Behind any invading force lies a council that commands from the rear. In this instance, it is the Court of the Seven-Headed Serpent, a group of Archdevils representing the seven deadly sins. The Covenant of Heaven and Hell ensures no true demon may walk the Earth, but the Serpent's heads are nothing if not ingenious. By mixing demons with creatures that walk the earth, both humans and animals, they have found ways to invade the material plane without incurring His retribution.

The Seven Heads of the Serpent are masters of the Sin they represent, each notorious and ruthless, gaining their power through deceit, treachery, or outright brutality. First amongst all is Eligos, the Duke of Petals, who sits at the head of the Council as the High Cathedra of Pride. Next is Mammon, the Prince of Greed, whose seat is adorned with gold and marble. At the seat of Lust sits Asmodeus, the Monarch of Lechery. Envy's seat is occupied by Moloch, the President of the Sacrificial Sun, whose idols are grander than Pride's. Next is Gluttony, which has seen stability again since Beelzebub’s abdication as Bael, the Uncrowned King of Stolen Land. The seat of Wrath, practical for one only concerned with destruction, is filled by Apollyon, the Lady of Locusts. Lastly, the Silk Bed of Sloth holds Belphagor, Duchess of the Gap, in slumber.

If the Court unites under a common goal for too long, Creation's fall is all but guaranteed.

The Defining Traits of Court 

Goetic Spells & Powers: The Sorcerer has harmed me once more.

What gives the Court its unique flavour, aside from running demons of hell, are the Goetic Powers that these demonic abominations possess. Goetic Powers are usually passive buffs, while Spells are Actions that require the caster to spend Sin Markers to power them. These Powers and Spells cover a broad range of buffs, including offensive, defensive, movement shenanigans, and utility options. Goetic Powers and Spells will be an important pillar of your playstyle, and they become even more important depending on your chosen Sin.

Hey There, Demons, It’s Me, Ya Boi

All but one of your possible units will have the Demonic Keyword, marking them as denizens of Hell. Since Hell is what may be considered "toasty" in the most optimistic way, its inhabitants are well-suited to the whole "Fire and Brimstone" thing and have adapted, and even thrived, in Hell's scorching environment. As a result, those with the Demonic Keyword do not suffer the effects of the Fire keyword. Fire is a pretty popular way to deal extra Blood Markers, so being immune to it helps you stay alive and in the game. You'll still struggle with Flamethrowers' Ignore Armour properties, but negating secondary Blood Markers is a huge advantage.

The Beatings Will Continue Until Morale Improves

While there are a variety of unique ways to generate Sin Markers, whipping your Wretched into shape remains a consistent, reliable way to generate what you need to power your Goetic Magiks. You won’t need to keep them locked away in a corner, receiving nothing but a paddlin’, but it’s still important to keep a Torture Instrument wielder nearby to get a few extra Sin Markers.

I Might Be Out of Spells, But I'm Not Out of Shells

Whilst Goetic Spells and Powers play a significant role in your game plan, they aren’t the only tool in the box. Like every faction, The Court get their own unique Battlekit items, with arguably some of the best Ranged and Melee Weapons in the game.  The Serpent Assault Gun, Ophidian Rifle, and Malabranche are perfect examples of powerful yet unique weapons that make The Court formidable on the battlefield. The variety only increases when you decide on a Sin.

Elected to Lead, Not to Read

Despite being the literal embodiment of Hell, your Elites will, more so than any other faction, be leading from the front. That may be mostly out of necessity, as your Wretched will be busy getting whipped into shape to generate Sin Markers. Still, your Elites pack not only Goetic abilities and game-changing weapons, but also some seriously stacked Profiles. Your Praetor and Desecrated Saint have multiple +3s on their profiles, for example, including the Tough keyword. The natural price of this is that you’re low on effective models. You'll have a few Wretched and Yoke Fiends, mostly for Sin Marker generation or on a back objective if required. That leaves the rest of your models, mostly your Elites, to get into the thick of it. They can do the job, but each loss hurts, and each mistake is punished. Still, you can use your Wretched activations to push back the need to activate your important units, so you’re not at a huge disadvantage compared to a truly low-model warband.

Battlekit Highlights

Arquebus: 8 Ducats

A simple gun for simple minds. Those being your Wretched and your Yoke Fiends. Its ability to double as a melee weapon makes it a cheap way to bring your throwaway models into your game plan, and at 18” range it will at least be able to reach out in the earlier parts of the game.

Chthonic Vessel: 1 Glory

This piece of Equipment is a Consumable that a single Elite may take. During a game, the bearer may instantly gain 2 Sin Markers. It’s a nice way to get a quick surge of Sin Markers exactly when you need them. Would be interesting to see on a Hunter, who is hungry for Sin Markers more often than not.

Crown of the Hellfire: 15 Ducats

Able to be equipped by Elites and the Pit locust; if equipped, it causes a Blood Marker to all enemy models within 1” of the model with this item at the end of its activation. It’s a nice piece of equipment, but not vital. Less so, since models with Negate Fire don't suffer the Blood Marker.

Fiendbound Gatling Gun; 20 Ducats

This 2-Handed weapon may not look particularly unique given its Heavy and Shrapnel keywords, but its ability sets it apart. The Excruciate ability lets a model with Strong, or a model in contact with another, Excruciate the gun, giving it the Automatic 2 and Reload Keywords. Getting a couple of shots off for 20 Ducats, with Shrapnel and being at 24” is pretty nice. The intention here is to have a Yoke Fiend and a Wretched side by side, letting the former unleash pot shots from afar while your big threats move up the board.

Iron Maildel Flail: 4 Glory

This Hell Knight only 2-handed melee weapon comes with +1 Dice, Cumbersome, and Heavy Keywords. Its special ability requires you to sacrifice one of your Wretched to be put inside the Iron Maiden. If you do, the Flail gets the Ignore Armour Keyword, and each time the Hell Knight makes a successful melee attack, it also gets a Sin Marker.

Jaws of Iron: 5 Ducats

The Jaws of Iron are a grenade that only your Yoke Fiends can carry. With a 6” range and a -1 Injury Dice, they’re not going to be taking out many enemies. However, that is not their purpose. They’re meant as a set-up piece so your Yoke Fiends can then charge in and attack in melee with an extra +1 Melee Dice, thanks to the Snap Shut ability on this weapon.

Restraining Muzzle: 10 Ducats

Another piece of Equipment exclusive to your Yoke Fiends. Up to 3 can take this, and it grants them a +1 Dice to Ranged Attack Rolls. It’s simple, though a little pricey compared to other factions' offerings.

Torture Instrument

A defining weapon of the Court, the trusty Torture Instrument keeps your Wretched where they belong: under the hoof and claw of Demons. This 2-handed weapon is primarily used to hit your own Wretched, thanks to the Torture Action ability, which allows the bearer to make a torture action instead of a Fight Action. This Action is similar, where the bearer makes a melee attack, but on a successful hit, the target is automatically taken down, and the model making the Action receives a Sin Marker. The Agonising Injuries ability reduces the amount of Dice used in an Injury roll to 1d6, with + or + Injury Dice still only resulting in the highest or lowest single Dice.

Serpent Assault Gun: 45 Ducats

This large “hand-cannon” (that actually needs two hands to wield it) shoots bullets enveloped in a stinky, but deadly gas at a range of 36”. By almost all accounts, the Serpent Assault Gun is the perfect gun. The long range, coupled with the Gas, Automatic 2 and Assault keyword, gives it some versatility for the wielder. The biggest drawback is that it is 2-handed, meaning you can’t take a Trench Shield with it. The Heavy keyword isn't great, but since you’ll most likely put this on something like a Praetor, it's largely moot. It costs a whopping 45 Ducats, but you are certainly getting your money's worth. As said, this is great on a Praetor, whose +3 Range stat makes fantastic use of this gun, even when not shooting at short range and/or into cover.

Malabranche Sword: 35 Ducats

The Malabranche Sword is in Melee what the Serpent Assault Gun is at Range. Namely, pure carnage. It’s less flashy than the SAG, but its simplicity keeps the focus on its sole objective: killing. The Malabranche Sword's defining characteristic is the Deadly Keyword. This keyword lets the user roll 3d6 on an injury roll and add the results together, rather than taking the top two. So you’re essentially getting a Blood Bath with every injury roll! The downside is you can only take one, and it costs 35 Ducats.

Ophidian Rifle: 25 Ducats

Back to the available range options, we have the Ophidian Rifle. Another long-range weapon at 30” of range, as well as being 2-handed, this rifle’s main ability is Unnatural Inversion. Instead of a -1 Dice when shooting at long range or at an enemy in cover, you instead gain +1 Dice. The Ignore Cover and Ignore Long Range keywords ensure you’re actually gaining this bonus. This Rifle is particularly strong on a Hell Knight, who can provide some early Blood Markers in the early rounds through combining the Unnatural Inversion ability with their built-in Blood Magic spell, which grants a +1 Injury Dice.

Headtaker: 15 Ducats

The assassin’s best friend. A simple one-handed melee weapon with no special keywords, but it provides a +2 Injury modifier if you target a model that hasn't activated yet. Be aware that it’s a flat modifier, with its pros and cons. Regardless, this is a great weapon for a Hunter of the Left-Hand Path, who can quickly get into melee thanks to their Left-Hand Path ability, even after following up a shot with their Bow of Lethe.

Yoke Fiends Credit: Darius Minis

Goetic Powers

Black Heart

A useful and cheap spell at 5 Ducats that grants a +1 Dice to the Success Roll the next time you make one. For 1 Sin Marker, it can certainly help ensure you do what needs to be done.

Blessing of the Serpent Moon

Basically the same as the previous interaction that was on the Sorcerer’s profile. Before an Injury Roll is made for a model with this Spell, you can add a -1 Injury Modifier for every 2 Sin Markers spent (up to 6). Keep those important units alive and kicking!

Infernal Challenge

Exclusive to the Hell Knights, this Ability adds +1 Injury Dice for Melee Attacks if the attacker's target has the Tough Keyword. Nice and simple, and at 10 Ducats, it’s not too expensive.

Raining Blood

After making a successful Spell action, you can place 1 Blood Marker on a number of enemy models equal to the number Sin Markers spent for this Spell (max 3), as long as those enemy models are within 18” of the Spellcaster. Important to note that Line of Sight is not needed!

Slavemaster

An Elite model can cast this spell for one Blood Marker and force a Yoke Fiend in 18” to perform one of the following commands:

  • Sacrifice: The Yoke Fiend kills itself (A bit extreme, but okay). 
  • Fight: Force the Yoke Fiend to make a Melee Attack.
  • Move: The Yoke Fiend moves, but no Charge or Retreat.
  • Shoot: Force a Yoke Fiend to make a Ranged Attack. 

The Yoke Fiend can still be activated as normal if it hasn't already been. It’s a nice ability that can mess with your opponent if you use it well.

The Units

Praetor: 115 Ducats

A demonic commander bound to serve a demon lord or archdevil. They command warbands in their master’s service, fulfilling whatever task they are given, whether that means fighting on the front lines of the Great War or taking part in the many battles within the realms of Hell itself, for Hell's power dynamics are ever-shifting. Despite their prowess and status in the Great War, they are seen in damnation as barely above even the mongrel Yoke Fiends; their mortal blood, however small, taints the demonic purity. The disgust they inspire in their patron is only just outweighed by their usefulness, as their mortal aspect lets them walk on His land.

The denizens of Hell may deem the Praetor meager and weak; on the table, however, it is anything but. The Praetor simply slaps in pretty much every respect. Stat-wise, it comes with 8” Flying movement, a +3 in both Melee and Ranged, and 0 native armour. Right off the bat, this stat profile is amazing. Whilst most leaders gain a paltry +2 in these stats, the Praetor cements its place as the king of leaders. They can, of course, take any Battlekit from the Court Armoury, as you might expect. Keyword-wise, they come with Elite, Fear, Strong and Tough. They also have the Demonic keyword (which almost all your warband has, bar the Wretched), granting them immunity to the effects of the Fire keyword. Lastly, for Sin Marker generation, they gain one any time they activate.

Sorcerer: 85 Ducats

Sorcerers have no predetermined appearance; each is as unique as the next, but all share the same levitating ability: their feet never touch the ground. They make excellent warband commanders in their own right, thanks to their cunning and Goetic traits, but they mostly serve as advisors to their Praetor overlords.

Stat-wise, the Sorcerer comes with a 6” flying movement and a +1 in Ranged and Melee. They may take any Battlekit from the Court Armoury, except for Ranged Weapons and Grenades. This may seem like an odd restriction, but they can make up for the lack of weapon-wielding with up to 3 powerful Goetic Spells. In addition to the 3 spells they choose, the Sorcerer comes with a built-in spell at no cost. Burning Inferno is a powerful ranged spell that grows more destructive the more Sin Markers you spend to fuel it. For their final ability, they may purchase the Leader Keyword for 5 Ducats.

Hunter of the Left-Hand Path

Experts in hunting the vile creatures that lurk within Hell, these hunters follow the Left-Hand path and use the still-living organs of their prey for their Goetic Magiks.

If the Praetor is your front-liner, tearing into the enemy with demonic ferocity, and your Sorcerer is your backliner, hurling fiery carnage, then the Hunter of the Left-Hand Path is your assassin, waiting for the right time to take out key enemy targets. They come with the standard 6” movement, but pack an amazing +2 in Ranged and +1 in melee. Battlekit-wise, they carry the Bow of Lethe at all times (since it's, kinda, you know, part of their arm and all that), and they can only carry one-handed weapons (again, the whole bow-arm thing explains that), and no shields.

The Bow of Lethe is a 24” one-handed Ranged Weapon that comes with the Assault keyword. The Special Ammunition keyword allows you to choose one of two bonuses before making an injury with this weapon: Either a +2 Injury Dice or Ignore Armour. This offers great versatility, letting you pick the right bonus for the enemy in sight.

But that is not all; the Hunter comes with some truly amazing Goetic Spells. First off is Left-Hand Path, which costs 2 Blood Markers. You use this Spell when the Hunter touches a terrain piece as part of a normal movement or Dash. You can remove them from the battlefield and place them touching another terrain piece within 24” and more than 1” away from enemy models. This will be your key assassin ability, letting you reach any model on the battlefield and truly play mind games with your opponent. To take this Spell up a notch, the Hunter comes with the Infiltrator keyword, meaning they can start outside your Deployment zone. The second Spell, Oracle Beast Cloak, is your defensive Spell if the enemy catches you. After paying a hefty 3 Blood Markers and an incoming Injury Roll is made, you can change that Injury Roll's result to “No Effect”. So even though you’re about to be sent back down to the pit, you can shrug it off and survive. Watch out, though: this Blood Marker is hungry, and you can only use it once a Turn. To ensure you never get caught out, you have Shadow-Walker, which lets you retreat for 2 Blood Markers without the enemy being able to make a Melee Attack against you.

Hell Knight: 100 Ducats

Hell Knights make up the bannerlets of a high lord of the Court. They are warriors of silent servitude and are called upon to fight when the followers of the Tyrant God foolishly believe they can thwart the inevitable.

Hell Knights have the usual 6” movement, with a +2 Dice only in Melee and a built-in -2 Armour thanks to their Infernal Iron Armour. This armor functions like Reinforced Armor, but adds the Impervious keyword, meaning its Armor bonus works even against weapons with the Ignore Armor keyword. As Elites, they can take any Battlekit from the Armoury. To top it off, they do come with the Demonic and Strong keywords. They lack Tough, but the Infernal Iron Armour provides ample protection unless your opponent gets lucky.

For Spells, the Hell Knight may take two Spells, but one must be their own Blood Magic Spell. For a cost of 1 Blood Marker, before making an Injury Roll, you may add +1 Injury Dice. Very simple, but very good, since it isn't limited to Melee attacks. Despite lacking a positive Ranged Characteristic, the Ophidian Rifle pairs well with the Hell Knight because of this Blood Magic Spell. As we’ll see later with the Lust Sin, you can get some deadly Ranged Damage with a Hell Knight and Ophidian Rifle. Lastly, Corpse Candles allows the Hell Knight to gain the Fear Keyword for 5 Ducats.

Wretched: 20 Ducats

Wretched are the souls whose humanity is not blessed by the demonic blood. The lowest rung of the infernal ladder, they serve as fodder on the front lines or as batteries to power the Goetic magic of their demonic overlords. However, should a Wretched strike down a worthy adversary, they may gain their freedom in memory and honour of the First Rebellion.

Let’s not beat around the bush here: on the table, Wretched reflect their namesake. They get the usual 6” movement, but have a negative Ranged and Melee characteristic, at -1 specifically. They may take any Battlekit from the Court Armoury, as long as it costs no more than 10 Ducats.

Goaded Forth is a neat ability that gives them a +1 Dice to their Dash Action, as long as they are within 8” and in Line of Sight of a Yoke Fiend. Their other ability is Law of Hell, which removes a Wretched from your Warband Roster should they take down an Elite.

The Wretched will be little more than batteries for your spells, but you can use them as fodder on the front lines after you have kitted out the main pieces in your warband. Be warned, though: you cannot have more Wretched than you do units with the Demonic keyword. So you can’t just swarm the board with Wretched and laugh like a maniac.

Yoke Fiend: 35 Ducats

Yoke Fiends are Demonic and Bestial Hybrids, grafted by the Priests of Hell. Coated in muscle and a mish-mash of animal features and traits, depending on how they were constructed. Despite their origins, they are formidable on the field, standing well above the meagre humans the faithful sacrifice to the Great War.

Stat-wise, you’ve got a typical 6” movement and a single +1 Dice in Melee. They may take a single Ranged Weapon for less than 30 Ducats, but may take anything else they want.

Their only ability is Glory Lost that adds +1 Dice to Melee Attacks made by a Yoke Fiend if there are 3 or more Sin Markers next to any number of friendly Yoke Fiends on the battlefield.

Pit Locust: 90 Points

Ferocious, horse-sized beasts, Pit Locusts are armoured behemoths whose faces are a disfigured mockery of a human. Feared even within Hell, they attack with blade forelimbs and a stinger on their tail. Despite all that, maybe they are the goodest of boys. If not friend, then why friend-shaped, right?

The Pit Locust is a fast-moving flanker that, despite their quick movement and flying, is quite tanky. The 8” Flying movement helps them get up the board, and the +1 Melee Characteristic helps them take down some weaker opponents. Lastly, the -2 Armour helps them survive longer than most. Unfortunately, they can’t take any Battlekit apart from the Crown of Hellfire, so you will need to rely solely on their melee attacks. Luckily, their Insectile Stingers ability lets them make two Melee Attacks with the Shrapnel keyword. While they may not be able to take down tougher targets, they can stack Blood Markers on an enemy, ready for another model of yours to bank them and secure a kill. Throw in a Crown of Hellfire, which gives all models within 1” a Blood Marker at the end of the activation, and you have a decent way to generate Blood Markers quickly.

Desecrated Saint: 140 Ducats

When Hell’s minions or champions are captured, they are taken to be locked away to be interrogated and experimented upon, where few mortals will set eyes on them. When a future Saint, Prophet, or other holy figure of the faithful is taken, however, they are proudly put on display, albeit in a new, more grotesque form.

This behemoth boasts the usual 6” Movement and a +3 in Melee and a native -3 Armour! It comes with Fear, Tough, and Strong, which will prove useful, as it has three hands, letting you wield a single two-handed weapon and two one-handed weapons, or three one-handed weapons.

Ability-wise, Annihilator allows you make one Fight Action for each Melee Weapon that the model is equipped with. Aura of Sin causes enemy models to be unable to benefit from their own friendly abilities, Actions or Special Rules for their Warband or Battlekit, excluding Ranged Attacks. It’s important  Relentless ignores the movement penalty when the Saint stands up after having been Downed. Lastly, Totemic grants a Sin Marker to a friendly Demonic model, should it have activated within 1” of the Saint.  The Saint is a great unit, but it suffers the same problem as the Praetor: its size. Whilst the Praetor can get up the board quicker, despite its 50mm base, the Saint not only sits on a 60mm base, but it also is the largest model in the game and only has a 6” movement. This will be drawing all the firepower your enemy can throw at it. Some of the sins can mitigate this weakness; however, for the most part, your Saint will struggle to get into the thick of things.

The Sins

We’ll be covering each Sin specifically in future articles, but for a brief overview, here’s what the vibe is in each of them: 

  • Pride: Pride is your Strength. Defiance is your purpose. Wield the Morningstar’s Light and armaments to bring your enemy to their knees. Use Open Terrain and elevation to your advantage, while keeping your Demonic units safe as your Wretched throw themselves in front of incoming enemy attacks. 
  • Greed: War has a price. A price that Mammon is all too happy to pay, for far greater riches can be gained. You gain Sin Markers by targeting certain priced units that decrease in threshold each Turn, and your Spells and Battlekit only work when affecting targets with a certain (Ducat) worth. 
  • Lust: Turn the Sin of the Flesh to your advantage; your mortal Non-Demonic Units can extract more Sin Markers. Battlekit and Powers ask you and your opponent how much they are willing to gamble to achieve their goals or avoid pain. 
  • Envy: Hell Knights envy those above them, and as such, Sorcerers and Praetors may not be taken in this warband. Instead, you may take 2 to 5 Hell Knights, gaining a unique Glorious Deed to use each game, as well as free Sin Markers for one of your Knights. You also generate Sin Markers for nearby allies by taking enemies out of Action or Downing them. Take your enemy's weapons as your own; why should you not covet such power? 
  • Gluttony: Indulge on your enemies as you wear them down with Melee attacks, culminating in a feast for your allies. Your Elites are harder to hit, and your hungry Troops are nimbler, as they look for their next meal. Your Powers and Battlekit aim to keep you alive and hungry for more. 
  • Wrath: Use the very fires of Hell to lay your enemies low; attacks with the Fire Keyword grant Sin Markers. Powers and Battlekit play around with the Fire Keyword, letting models add it to all their Melee Attacks, or even turn the ground itself to fire. 
  • Sloth: Ensure inevitable victory by converting your Success rolls into Risky Success Rolls, and slowing your opponent's tempo. Your Spells and Battlekit punish enemy models that have already activated and pull them out of position.

Final Thoughts

So, there we have it! Court is one of the most rewarding factions to play; like New Antioch, you need to use every part of a unit's activation to juggle objective capture, board control, and taking out important targets, all with a very small effective model count. If you pull it off, you may just find yourself at the seat of the table.

title: Old Faerie MTG card spikes 530% thanks to underrated competitive combos
content:
The Shadowmoor Magic: The Gathering card Knacksaw Clique is getting seriously expensive. Regular copies have gone from $2.80 back in August, to over $18 today. Meanwhile, foils have been selling for as much as $200, even if they're not in mint condition. TCGPlayer lists very few sales for these foil Cliques, incidentally, suggesting the supply is already pretty low.

As a rare card from an older set, and a faerie at that, this card was always liable to spike if the right synergies came along. It seems like its time is here, but surprisingly the format that seems responsible for this spike is actually cEDH - not where we normally look for big market drivers.

Even weirder, there's no new cards at all making this one spike. Instead, it's an infinite combo that already existed, but seems to have been undervalued up until now. However, in the last few months Kinnan, Bonder Prodigy decks featuring Knacksaw Clique have topped several cEDH tournaments, including the 80-player Topdeck Invitational back in August.

Since Knacksaw Clique has an untap ability, it's fairly easy to make its ability go infinite. You just need a way to make the creature tap for mana. With Paradise Mantle equipped or Cryptolith Rites on the board, Knacksaw Clique can tap for one blue mana, and with Kinnan in play that becomes two. Then you're free to mill all of your opponents down to nothing.

The combo is very versatile, with multiple cards that can make it work. For instance, you can use it even if Kinnan isn't available, with a card like Training Grounds to reduce the activated ability cost to one, which then means you don't need his mana doubling.

While it's not new, it seems fans have gained a new appreciation for the combo, or perhaps someone just decided to buy out the supply after the tournament wins? What's funny to me is that people have been calling Knacksaw Clique underrated for quite literally a decade.

Either way, if the hype dies down we might expect to see its price fall somewhat, but given how few copies are around, it'll probably remain fairly expensive if it doesn't get an eventual reprint.

Welcome back, Dear Reader, to my ongoing blog of hobby and competitive play progress through 2026. Last week I talked about my plans for the 2026 Grand Narrative and World Championships of Warhammer, how I'm planning to paint and build armies for both, and how I might tackle those hobby challenges. This week I'm setting that plan in motion, starting with some test games and more hobby progress on my Red Corsairs, who kind of became my key hobby project for 2026.

Getting in Some Practice

Over the last few weeks I've been kind of snowed in writing content updates in the wake of the September 2026 Balance Update, which released alongside the new Codex: Space Marines and more or less upended the entire game with stats and points updates to every marine faction. I've been looking through results over the last few weeks, updating Detachment Focus articles (like Cabal of Chaos), and thinking about how I might want to tackle list building in the latter half of the year. While my operating plan is currently to work on Emperor's Children for worlds, I have Red Corsairs in front of me right now for the Grand Narrative.

For the most part, the toughness changes don't seem to matter that much. They matter in the context of being shot/attacked by other marines, but a lot of weapons went to S5 to compensate for this change, making some (power weapons) comparatively worse, and keeping wound values fairly similar. Terminators being at T6 is interesting, but it's not a particularly common breakpoint. one of the funniest parts of this is honestly that there are now very few T4 units in the game.

What does matter however is having S5, AP-1 bolters. Specifically combi-bolters. I made entire Top cuts happen on the back of Scarab Occult Terminators having massed quantities of AP-2 shooting, and that's replicable on the cheap with CSM terminators now - you can combine terminators with S5 AP-1 bolters with Sorcerers in Terminator Armour to give a target +1 AP on incoming attacks, and when the Terminators do their Dark Pact for Sustained or Lethal Hits (a key part of the Tsons sorcerer), they automatically get to re-roll their to hit rolls. As an extra bonus, they get +1 Strength on their bolters (to S6) when shooting in Cabal of Chaos thanks to being a [PSYKER] unit.

That's a solid base. Using that, I put together this list:

It's a little wonky, and not likely to be what I actually take to the Grand Narrative. For one, I'm unlikely to bring Huron to the event. I may have the model on hand but I tend to think having named characters at the Grand Narrative is kind of lame. Huron's got his own shit going on, he wouldn't be slumming it with my guys. I may still bring the Masters of the Maelstrom, though - they're a bit more instrumental to building playable lists in 11th edition and they're painted very well. Fabius is a bit more of a wild card here as well in that regard - he's a named character but again, I don't think you can build great lists without him so I'm on the fence there. May also depend on my ability to get more guys painted. We'll see.

The general idea here is the Terminators drop in and shoot things to death. The unit with Huron is OC +1, which makes them good Take and Hold objective holders, plus they have a reactive move (and VotLW gives me a second to play with). The Bikes and Red Corsairs Raiders are my forward action units/objective holders, and the Chosen are my third big threat in the army. There's also a Nemesis Claw. I painted them. And they're a [PSYKER] unit, which is pretty funny. It lets them do fun stuff with the Detachment. That's more a bad unit I'm taking because they're painted well, but they have some solid utility.

I need to start getting in some good WCW practice as well, so I called up my buddy Garrett Moore, who you can find occasionally writing some stellar content for our Subscriber-only service. The Wolf-Touched Bike Captain is the real capital-N Nasty Shit in this list, joining a large unit of Wulfen to give them extra movement (thanks to the MOUNTED keyword) on top of the ability to Advance and Charge but the Thunderwolves and Outriders are also cracked here, moving 14" in Stormlance before they advance and charge, and all of the units I just mentioned can auto-advance 6" before they charge. This list has me terrified, partly because it just seems like what I'm doing but better in every way, and partly because it has just way too many units for what it seems like it should have - you have four massive threats: Wulfen, Grimnar + Wolf Guard, and two big units of Thunderwolves, and then you still have eight units on top of that, giving you lots of fast ability to spread out and dominate the table. I am legitimately worried I won't be able to deep strike if I don't go first, and even then it's a crap shoot.

The Mission: Take and Hold Mirror - Battlefield Dominance

I'm going first. Which is good here, because even though I want to react to Garrett, I need to get deep strikers down before he eats the entire fucking table. My plan is to try and drop after him as much as possible - I need my units to come in and kill key threats, not get charged. I put the Nemesis Claw in reserves by accident (forgot to deploy them), along with both units of Terminators. Terminators being 370 points in CSM is a neat benefit.

I draw Outflank and Burden on turn 1 and pass the turn. I'll score 4 for Burden at the end of his turn. Garrett plays cagey on his turn as well, trying to avoid getting alpha struck. He can play aggressively with his Eradicators and Impulsors, because the idea is to drop the Eradicators and bring the Impulsors up to try and move block me aggressively, pinning me in my Deployment Zone early. On my second turn I draw Secure No Man's Land and Behind Enemy Lines. I'm not able to steal the middle objective for Secure, but I kill Garrett's Impulsor to stop it from gumming up my end of the table and score Outflank with my Nemesis Claw.

It's around this point that I notice we aren't really playing the same game when it comes to Command points. It's the bottom of turn 2, and I've spent one Command point, and I look over at the totals:

What the fuck are we even doing here? Garrett is getting extra command points essentially for free and getting them at the start of the battle round. I cannot stress enough that making this "if your warlord is on the table" rule should just be a game rule and not something rolled out in codexes. It is incredibly tedious to play against if you're not a codex haver and feels completely busted. In part because it meant Garrett never had to even think about discarding a secondary for CP - why would he, when doing so provides no value?

I end up struggling to drop second against Garrett. My big plan - dropping the Terminators via Ingress to hit is Thunderwolves after a charge - gets ruined when he re-rolls his charge roll for them into an 11 and just smashes into my Terminators, no problem. I'll lose half of them to the now 3 damage Thunderwolf melee attacks before clapping back, and Huron will just roll incredibly disappointingly to ensure one of the cavalry lives. I'll fall back and kill him with other units.

On the other side of the table I get a fun little reminder that no, we aren't playing the same game when my three bikes go up against Garrett's. For the same points cost (80), marine bikes get 4 wounds apiece instead of 3, have BS 2+ bolters with [ASSAULT] and [TWIN-LINKED] and they get [SUSTAINED HITS] and either +1 to hit on their thunder hammers or +1 damage on their other melee weapons when they charge. Again: What the fuck are we doing here?

The real brutal game-ender of a turn happens when I fail a 3" charge with my raiders into the scouts at mid-table (seen above), then on the following turn attempt to take out the Thunderwolves with Terminator Shooting. My Terminator Sorcerer fails his psychic test roll and takes 3 mortal wounds on the unit, killing a model and getting no AP debuff. Ok, fine it happens. Then my other Terminator Sorcerer attempts the same thing and also fails, letting Garrett drop Armour of Contempt to just shrug off the damage and keep his TWC unit alive.

Ultimately I'm out of units before Grimnar even hits the table in a meaningful fashion. I've managed to take out the Wulfen and the TWCs but there's still a ton on the table and I was only ever able to deep strike in my own Deployment zone - a brutal combo for an army that needs to drop in and shoot. Having attempted this with Veterans, I think the smart play is to switch to Warpstrike Champions. There's more value there, and being able to pick back up is a big benefit I'm just kind of missing.

Result: 95-58, Loss

This was a brutal loss because it felt unwinnable at the outset and I'm not sure what my counterplay is. I think I need to retool completely and work on a Warpstrike Champions list that runs different units - it may be time for Mutilators, though I don't love the idea of putting them in here. That said, I could definitely do a set that are based on Assault Centurions, and that seems really cool conceptually, now that I think about it. Stay tuned.

Hobby Progresss

My big focus right now is on my Red Corsairs. I need to get them done in time for the Grand Narrative, which is about a month away. They're in good shape already, and I'm thinking about how I might want to do some of these units and hit on bigger centerpiece models. My Dallas lads are all still around, and I need to finish the following at least:

  • 2 Red Corsairs Raiders (I have 8/10 painted)
  • 5 Red Corsairs Chosen (converted using Raiders models)

On top of that, I have some stretch goals:

  • 5 Red Corsairs Terminators
  • 5 Red Corsairs Warp Talons
  • 2 Red Corsairs Predators
  • Red Corsairs Multilators

Those stretch goals I'll take as I can. On the topic of the two Raiders, I got those painted over the weekend:

This guy's done, but I also had another I was doing, and it turned out I'd forgotten to do a second meltagun in the unit, so I had to model him holding one, and did a strap for it out of green stuff. I think it turned out great:

Then there's this guy, the first of my Red Corsairs Chosen. The idea here is to use Raiders bodies with the arms and heads of Chosen, to give them the right wargear and to give them a bit more of a "Chaos touch."

I'm really happy with this guy and working on the next four, as well as the Warp Talons. They're converted from Mk. VI jump units, using Warp Talon bits and Vanguard Veteran lightning claws. I like how they look so far- very much in line with the aesthetic I'm going for here.

The Tone Pro paints are really nice on these, giving me a nice, saturated red that blends easily with layering. I've been enjoying using them for my newer models. I'm going to finish painting this guy, see how I like him, then figure out my plan for the rest.

Final Thoughts

That's it for this week. Next week it'll be more painting and hopefully another game in but I have my work cut out for me. I'm really not sure what I can do at the moment to compete in the new marine/Ork meta but I'm sure some things will emerge soon and I'll focus on copying what works in those areas. Only poorly, and tailored to my ability to paint units in time for the World Championships.

See you Thursday.

title: Hextoricals: Coast Watchers
content:
The Australian coast watchers played a crucial role in the Pacific Theater, providing intel within the campaigns for the Solomons and New Guinea, at great personal peril: Many of these coast watchers were captured and executed by the Japanese as spies, but their sacrifice allowed the Allies to have ample warning of Japanese build up and operations, sighting both airplanes and ships and signaling their approach. Initially they’d been set up as intel operation within the various islands of the Pacific Ocean, but the blistering fast pace of the Japanese advance meant that they quickly found themselves behind enemy lines.

Will you take the role of the coast watchers and provide crucial intel for the Allied fleets, or will you command the Japanese patrols that are hunting them down?

Coast Watchers is the first game in GMT’s new Recon Series and simulates the struggles of the Australian coast watchers during the invasions (and eventual recapture) of the Solomons, Guadalcanal and New Guinea. Designed by Volko Ruhnke, of COIN fame, the game showcases his love for asymmetrical conflicts and hidden information, and there are clear inspirations from both Labyrinth and the COIN games interwoven within this design.

The main conceit of the game is one of bluffs, double bluffs and a cat-and-mouse game of trying to keep your coast watchers hidden on one side, and trying to find them and capture them on the other. Both sides have information that is hidden from the other, so neither has a full picture of what exactly is going on, or what their opponent intends to do. Coast Watchers is also singularly focused on the gathering of intel and information, and a scenario ends as soon as the Japanese run their military operations: There is no capturing terrain in this game, as those are the concerns of other forces and other games.

Unboxing and Materials

As expected from GMT, this is a beautifully produced game: The board especially is notable, as it has recesses for the Allied pieces (which are the green wooden blocks). This isn’t just a way to mark where they should be placed, but also makes them less likely to be knocked away or flipped: Since this is a hidden information game, a moment of clumsiness that reveals a piece might spoil a particular playthrough.

Everything inside the box, apart from the player aids, rulebook and playbook. Credits: Riccardo Fabris

The green wooden blocks are similarly of a high standard, with embossed, illustrated sides that represent empty stations, or ones inhabited by coast watchers, refugees, downed airmen or even guerillas. The Japanese forces are mostly represented by counters: There are patrol markers, with Army patrols on one side and Police patrols on the other (the latter being more effective since the Japanese are working in conjunction with local forces). There are also counters marking Japanese-occupied bases or sites, which, on the reverse either show a quiet location or a build up of some kind, the latter being required in order for the Japanese player to run their operations. The Allies, once they have found these build-ups, have their own report markers to make note of what they found.

Other components include different types of cards: Mission and Asset cards for both sides, as well as two solitaire decks that allow the game to be played alone either on the Allied side or the Japanese side. Along with two player aids, there is a solitaire aid, and various scenario sheets, marked from A to H, which give instructions on how to set up the game and which special rules each scenario has: The scenarios range from the very start of the Japanese invasion to the eventual retaking of Rabaul, the main Japanese base in the area.

Finally, there are two boards for the Delivery and Patrol chits (although you will have to provide your own cups), and a rulebook and playbook, with the latter outlining the intricate operations and missions that could occur in the scenarios of the game.

Gameplay

As befits the theme, Coast Watchers is a game about finding information: The main aim of the Allied players is locating the Japanese build up as a prelude to their operations, and placing their coast watchers in the path of these eventual operations in order to give ample warning to the Allied bases that are being targeted. On the other hand, the Japanese player is on the hunt for the coast watchers, trying to locate and capture them, both to prevent them from spotting the build up as well as clearing a path for their invasion fleets or air raids.

Since both sides have hidden information about their forces, many actions within the game force one side or the other to close their eyes while their opponent changes the state of the board: In many situations, you might not even know the location of where your opponent made their move, which is something quite unique, at least in the world of board wargames. Even the setup of a simple scenario requires the Japanese player to close their eyes, as the Allied player distributes their initial allotment of coast watchers at various locations on the board: Many of their blocks will be palm leaves, signifying an empty station, but some of them will hide coast watchers, and often times, depending on the scenario, either refugees or downed airmen that need to be rescued.

The coast watchers are on the back foot as several of their stations are revealed. Credits: Riccardo Fabris

The different scenarios, along with having different set up instructions, can also have a maximum of three or five turns: The end of a particular game of Coast Watchers is in the hands of the Japanese player, since they get to decide when they run their operations, which means that even a five turn scenario can potentially earlier, even on turn two on occasion.

The flow of a turn starts with the Japanese preparations phase, where they can either gain new assets (which provide abilities that allow them to hunt down the coast watchers more effectively), they can ready patrols for use during the turn, or they can secretly add build ups to their bases and sites: The latter action is dictated by the kind of missions that they drew at the start of the scenario, with the pool of potential missions being set by the scenario instructions.

Once they have finished their preparations, it is the time for the Allied activities phase. They get a total of five actions that they can perform: Delivery, operate, evade and train. Although the Allied player is free to do as many of each type of action as they wish, they have to follow the order above; all deliveries must be completed before any operational action is performed, and so on. Delivery requires the use of assets, representing airplanes, small boats or even submarines, and can be used to either send supplies to your coast watchers, rescue refugees and downed airmen or insert new coast watchers that have been previously trained: Deliveries in Japanese-held areas are risky, however, and run the danger of being spotted or even prevented outright. This is done by placing a specific number of chits within the Delivery cup and then drawing two of them; drawing one or more “spotted” chits will force you to reveal your forces and allow any Japanese patrols to attempt to capture them.

Initial setup for one of the many scenarios. Credits: Riccardo Fabris

Operate actions allow the coast watchers to either observe build ups if they successfully avoid Japanese patrols, or even strike out and ambush Japanese soldiers if they have guerillas and the required asset card. Evade actions allow your revealed coast watchers to become hidden again: If they are revealed, many actions are simply not possible, and being revealed makes it easier for the Japanese player to capture your pieces. Finally, train actions allow you to get more coast watchers ready for deployment in future turns.

Once the Allies have finished their activities phase, the Japanese’s countermeasures phase starts: They also get 5 actions which need to be done in a strict sequence; Recall, Search and Deploy. Recall allows them to return patrols on the map to their ready area (usually done when a station is deactivated due to the capture of a coast watcher). Search is the main way that the Japanese player can strike back at the coast watchers: This is where the Patrol Cup comes into play.

Unlike the Delivery Cup, the Patrol Cup is not reseeded each time that it’s used: Instead, the ratio of chits within it is updated throughout the game. It contains either Japanese patrols, or Allied evasion chits, and when a search is conducted in a location, the Japanese player draws a number of chits depending on what kind of patrol they have in that location (either army or police patrols): The more patrol chits you draw from the cup, the more likely you are to find the coast watchers, or even capture them outright. Crucially, a location can only be searched once per phase, so if the coast watchers are revealed (but not captured), it’s possible for the Allied player to hide them again before the Japanese player is able to capture them..

Another scenario set up and ready to play. Credits: Riccardo Fabris

The final action available to the Japanese player is Deploy: They can either place patrols from their ready area to the Patrol Cup, or place them on the board itself. It’s important to strike a balance between enough patrols on the board versus having patrols in the cup, since the latter makes it more likely that any individual search will be successful.

The countermeasures phase is followed by another Allied activities phase, which is exactly the same as the first. Once the allies have finished their second activities phase, the Japanese player has a choice: They can either immediately run their operations, which signals the end of the game (although this decision is forced on the last turn of a particular scenario), or they can perform an additional countermeasures phase.

If they do elect to run operations, they immediately reveal their build up and mission cards: Some of the missions will require them to set a path from the build ups to their targets, while other missions simply require the build up to be present in a specific location. Once they have set these paths, the Allied player reveals their remaining coast watchers, and then both sides total up the number of points they receive: The Japanese player receiving points for performing their operations and missions and capturing Allied pieces, and the Allied player getting points for accurately reporting the location of Japanese build up, for having coast watchers on the way of a particular operation, or for rescuing refugees and airmen. Once both sides have summed their points, whoever scored the most wins the scenario!

A zoom into the Bismarks and New Britain areas. Credits: Riccardo Fabris

The above might seem quite complex at first glance, but in actual play the game tends to be quite a smooth experience, although the final tallying of points can be somewhat of a chore, since there are many discrete sources of points on both sides, which can often lead to mistakes. The game does feel rather unique and the marriage of ideas and inspiration from COINs and hidden movement games makes the entire package quite novel and unexpected.

The game does feature a way to play both sides solitaire, which is welcome, and there was clearly a lot of effort involved in trying to make both sides playable, although it is clear that the design was intended as a two player experience first and foremost.

Historicity

Although I’ve read quite a few books centered around the Pacific Theater, the role of the coast watchers within the Solomons and New Guinea campaigns has always been somewhat of a footnote: There are plenty of mentions of them helping the war effort, and even outlines of the extreme levels of duress that they and the civilians that helped them went through during the war. But even then there is a distinct lack of detail in most books about the accounts and experiences of these men as they struggled to survive. The game does a lot to outline and explain the history of the coast watchers, especially within the playbook, and I think it should be complimented for this alone: The history of the coast watchers is a history worthy of being told and remembered.

On the other hand, the game doesn’t really reflect the experiences of the individual coast watchers, and puts you in the shoes of the people that either ran the program on the Allied side or coordinated the attempts to hunt them down on the Japanese side. This zoomed out perspective does create somewhat of a detachment from the troops on the ground, since you are looking at a much wider picture than the singular struggle to survive, and the abstraction required for the game to be at this particular scale does diminish, at least for me, the impact of the stories that the game is trying to tell.

Critiques & Quirks

Of all of the GMT games that I’ve reviewed so far, I think this is probably going to be the one I’m most critical of, since I think there are issues with the game that outright prevent me from giving a seal of approval to Coast Watchers.

One of the main issues with the game is that its core gameplay loop feels like you are playing a game of whack-a-mole on repeat, something that is not singular to this game but tended to plague the games in the COIN series as well, although I will argue that the issue is far worse in Coast Watchers than it is in any of the COIN games, even the ones that are strictly for two players only. Much like the insurgent factions in COIN games, Allied pieces in this game can either be revealed or hidden, with the latter making them much harder to remove and also allowing them to perform several actions. This can lead to situations in either series where one side reveals the enemy pieces, is unable to remove them once revealed, and the other side counters by hiding them again. Repeat ad infinitum.

COIN games somewhat alleviate this issue since usually there are more than 2 players at the table, and the turn order can be randomly decided based on the cards drawn. Sides also usually have a limited number of resources they can expend. Finally, special operations or newly acquired capabilities that are unique to each side can swing the fight decisively one way or the other. Finally, there are sometimes other obligations or actions that either side might want to take instead of simply finding or hiding their troops.

New Britain and New Guinea. Credits: Riccardo Fabris

Coast Watchers has none of those release valves. The primary aim of the Japanese player is to simply search and find the coast watchers: The entire countermeasures phase is centered around that. There are ways to stack the deck in your favour, by seeding the patrol cup or finding specific assets, but those options will eat up valuable actions either during the preparation or countermeasures phase: Instant capture is also not possible unless you have police patrols, which require either to be present in the starting set up, or as upgrades thanks to the capture of other coast watchers, or just randomly found as an asset draw.

Now, revealing coast watchers does force the Allied player to waste actions to Evade them, and might prevent them from delivering more supplies and coast watchers, but especially at the end of the game, the Allied player might gather enough points simply by the presence of their coast watchers in crucial areas, and thus won’t care if they are not able to do any actions.

This has led to games as the Japanese where, even though I was pressuring my opponent as much as I could, and I had stacked both the patrol cup and had police patrols in place, I wasn’t able to capture the coast watchers simply because I didn’t get the draws that I needed. The game can reach a state where bluffing is not really required any more, and the two players are mechanically just hoping that luck swings their way and they get the draws that they require to win against their opponent.

This issue is more acute within the more limited 3 turn scenarios, where the Japanese player simply does not have the time to stack the odds against the Allied player enough to pressure them into making risky supply deliveries. Although I did enjoy the 5 turn scenarios more, and there was more scope for double bluffs, the gameplay loop still didn’t really engage me as much as I hoped it would.

This is not to say that the game doesn’t have a deep level of strategy or analysis: The playbook features entire pages that outline the possible combinations of missions and operations that the Japanese can take for each individual scenario, and it’s clear that a lot of thought went into how each scenario is balanced. Despite this, the immediate loop of the game did not enthrall me.

I think the issues with this loop are even more pronounced within the solitaire version of the game. Although the solitaire decks for either side do an admirable job of trying to simulate the decision-making of an actual opponent, the solitaire game felt laborious, and lacked that distinct level of mind-games that made the base game at least somewhat enjoyable. It really brought to the forefront the issues with the loop as presented.

Finally, I do have issues with how the rulebook is written. I have a tendency to prefer games that have a very procedural and technical layout: The Coast Watchers rulebook is meant more as a play guide, and I had difficulties referencing particular rules due to its layout. This is not to say that the rulebook is obtuse or that the rules are unclear, however, and this criticism is more of a personal preference more than anything else.

Final Thoughts

Considering my criticisms listed above, I would be hard pressed to recommend this game. After playing through multiple scenarios, both against other players and solitaire, the core gameplay loop felt very similar between them and it wasn’t one that I really enjoyed going through. On the other hand, the game is very novel and is definitely attempting to push the boundaries of board wargames, and I think for someone that is interested in the Pacific Theater (and, especially, about a relatively little-known part of that conflict) and also likes hidden movement games like Fury of Dracula and other such board games, there is more than enough longevity within this game to whet their appetite. Unfortunately, from my own perspective, I cannot personally recommend such an expensive purchase.

title: Folk horror miniature skirmish game sees pilgrims fighting with faith
content:
Set in "a new world that was never meant to be found", Pilgrim: The Haunted Frontier is a folk horror miniature skirmish game where players work together, controlling pilgrims fending off terrifying monsters in the woods. With the game's first scenario out now for free and a Gamefound crowdfunder on the way, we spoke to the designer (and Buer Games cofounder) Eric Michael Robinson to find out more.

"I only want to make games with worlds I really want to dive deep into," Robinson says. Buer's other titles - Carnivore, set in the desperate cataclysm of the end-Cretaceous mass extinction, and 1490 Doom, set in a medieval apocalypse - go hard on aesthetics, and Pilgrim is no exception. It's also, like the others, not a cheery game.

"There's something compelling about a group of people leaving home to cross an ocean to start a new life in a new land," says Robinson. "The game's goal is to immerse the player in a really fun experience exploring an unknown land filled with terrifying horrors. There's mystery, discovery, side plots, and really spooky minis. I love playing cooperative games and this felt like a great setting for solo or co-op play."

Instead of HP, the key stats for surviving the dangers of Pilgrim is Faith. The demo scenario sees players contending with shades on the seashore, who can drain a pilgrim's faith just by getting close. Lose it all, and there's a ticking clock before that character is lost to madness. And since there are only seven named pilgrims in the game, all with unique abilities, that's probably not a good thing.

"The faith mechanic is very prominent as the Pilgrims go deeper into the woods and experience more horrors," says the creator. "They use Faith to reroll failed rolls but Pilgrims must be careful not to use it all, or they become susceptible to drifting into the woods and being claimed."

While the game's Wendigo (who appears on the front cover) reminds us of the beast from The Ritual, Robinson gives a surprising source when asked for media that inspired the game: Over the Garden Wall. "That show is perfect in my opinion. That idea of the unknown very much influenced the mystery of Pilgrim's world."

Eric says Pilgrim shares some similarities with Joseph McCollough's Rangers of Shadow Deep, another co-op skirmish game where you venture into the dark with a band of cohorts, but says the two have very different mechanics.

With immersion-setting music and evocative art and minis, the Pilgrim looks set to be a truly spooky game. We don't yet have a release date or Gamefound launch, though Buer Games has a preview event planned for October 28.

Come join the Wargamer Discord to chat more about this game and many like it!

title: D&D reveals new batch of monsters designed by kids
content:
After a three year gap, Wizards of the Coast has revealed Volume Two of Misplaced Monsters, a miniature menagerie of D&D monsters designed by miniature humans: or, as they're often called, children.

Releasing on December 2, 2026, Misplaced Monsters: Vol 2 is a collection of eight monsters designed to support a charity, with all proceeds "100% of the sales price" going to Seattle Children's Hospital's mental and behavioral health programs.

A relatively small expansion, the volume contains eight monsters and one magic item and is priced at $7.95. Like the old Extra Life Magic: The Gathering Secret Lairs, a major part of the appeal (apart from giving to charity) is that you get to see the children's art side by side with professional artists' recreations of that art.

In fact, Wizards has shared the pics on social media, so we can see exactly what is in this product. There's an interesting mix: some blobs, a dire elephant seal, and 'Minnie' who looks like a regular cat, but presumably is not.

Here's the full list of monsters:

  • Elea the Monster
  • Dire Elephant Seal
  • Minnie
  • Octo-Plus
  • Retanglosaurus
  • Pengu-Z
  • Chroapicosoa
  • Monster Ball

No clues have been given about the magic item though.

If this lot are anything like the batch of Misplaced Monsters from 2023, which included a dragon that dealt blueberry damage, there'll be plenty of weirdness in here. You can also buy the two packs together, for 14 monsters in total.

title: This is MTG Universes Beyond's laziest trick and I hate it
content:
At the Magic: The Gathering Star Trek debut on Monday, there were several cards I liked, and one that made me roll my eyes so hard I may have actually damaged something. That card was Seven of Nine, Unassimilated, and I bet you can already guess why I don't like it.

Yes, it's the transformation ability that gives her a 7/9 statline that irks me. The rest of the card is absolutely fine. She's got an ability related to differently named lands, representing exploration, and she loots, representing accumulated knowledge. Then she gets stronger from all that exploration, I guess. It doesn't have much to do with Seven of Nine's journey in particular, I think, and would arguably work for literally any Star Trek character with a story arc, but ho hum.

I'm in danger of making a mountain out of a molehill here, but I just find Magic's habit of spotting a number in a character's name and then building the card around that number so damn dull. It feels lazy, corny even, and makes it seem like the designers are just phoning it in.

They've done it so many times now, too. From the Ten Rings to Doctor Octopus, Eleven to The Fantastic Four, and I hate it every single time. This isn't even the only example in this set - they also gave Deep Space 9, 9/9 stats and a station and mana cost of 9.

At its best, Universes Beyond incorporates and adapts the characteristics of our favorite franchises into the game system that is Magic: The Gathering. From a Weeping Angel becoming a harmless artifact when you play a creature to Boromir sacrificing himself to save your other creatures, it feels great to see these moments and characters thoughtfully encapsulated on a card.

I don't mind when they get cute with it, either, like using reminder text so Shadowfax can show us the meaning of haste or the split-second mechanic to represent pausing the game so you can do some Fallout Inventory Management.

But just slapping numbers onto stuff doesn't do this. Seven of Nine's character has nothing to do with the numbers seven and nine, just as Eleven's character has nothing to do with the number 11. I really don't see who this is for. Surely this doesn't please fans of the character or Magic fans. The joke is overplayed, no one thinks it's clever anymore

I genuinely would prefer this card if it was exactly the same, but became an 8/8 instead.

title: MTG Commander banlist 2026
content:
Looking for the MTG Commander banlist? Commander is a vast, powerful, and ever-changing format, so it's crucial to stay on top of card bans. If you need a quick reminder of which cards can and can't go in your favorite deck, here's a complete list of Commander bans, from the latest to the very first.

So far, there have been 83 banned cards in MTG's Commander format. Use the links below to check out the latest changes and updates; the full banlist; or Wizards' new system of Game Changers and play brackets in EDH, explained. For more bans in other formats, see our full MTG banlist tracker.

  • Latest Commander banlist update
  • Full Commander banlist
  • Game Changers list
  • Brackets explained

Latest Commander banlist update

On February 9, 2026, Wizards of the Coast unbanned two Commander cards:

  • Biorhythm
  • Lutri, the Spellchaser (except as Companion)

Lutri's case is obvious - it was only banned because it could serve as a Companion in any deck.

The decision to make a new designation 'banned as Companion' appeared to weigh heavily on the designers, based on Gavin Verhey's article - adding sub-lists increases complexity and the chance that players will bring a card in a slot it's not supposed to. The decision was deemed acceptable because the worst case scenario for player mistakes isn't that bad - you tell the player with Lutri in the companion slot that he's banned, and they drop him into the 99.

Because Lutri was banned for reasons not really related to power he bypassed the gamechangers list, where unbanned cards typically go.

Meanwhile, Biorhythm was unbanned following a trend of unbanning expensive, high-impact cards that have a big impact on the game. If Worldfire and Coalition Victory can be legal cards without messing up the format too much, so can Biorhythm.

Full Commander banlist

(8 of) The Power 9

  • Ancestral Recall - banned April 2005
  • Black Lotus - banned April 2005
  • Mox Emerald - banned April 2005
  • Mox Jet - banned April 2005
  • Mox Pearl - banned April 2005
  • Mox Ruby - banned April 2005
  • Mox Sapphire - banned April 2005
  • Time Walk - banned April 2005

It's no surprise to see these here. If any card was going to be banned in Commander, it would be the Power 9 - some of the most broken cards ever made in Magic, each offering absurd value for their mana cost.

Speaking of cost, what's interesting is that it was their price point, not their power level, that originally saw these cards consigned to the Commander banlist - in the very first spate of bannings back in 2005.

The RC was worried that these cards would auto-includes for anyone wanting a really strong deck, and didn't want the fan-made format to have a perceived budget of thousands of dollars.

You might notice only 8/9ths of the Power 9 is actually banned. Timetwister is really an honorary member of the gang - it's busted when played with cards from the other 8. But in fact, a wheel, even a really great wheel like Timetwister, isn't worth making a fuss about.

Broken in the format

  • Limited Resources - banned June 2008
  • Channel - banned April 2005
  • Fastbond - banned June 2009
  • Trade Secrets - banned April 2013
  • Griselbrand - banned June 2012
  • Karakas - banned September 2008
  • Lutri, the Spellchaser - banned as companion February 2026
  • Yawgmoth's Bargain - banned May 2006

These cards are all banned because their designs are unbalanced in the context of EDH. Some, like Channel and Yawgmoth's Bargain, use life as a resource - one that's far more abundant when you start on 40. Others work poorly with multiple players. For instance, Trade Secrets allows two players to collude against the others for a runaway advantage, while Limited Resources stops anyone playing more than two to three lands.

Finally, Lutri is only banned as a companion - because the singleton nature of the format means he could (and therefore, optimally, should) be a companion for any red/blue deck.

It's almost refreshing to see these designs - memories of a time before every card was designed for Commander.

Dexterity cards

  • Chaos Orb - banned June 2010
  • Falling Star - banned April 2005

These feel more like unset cards, and wouldn't be printed without the acorn stamp today. The RC didn't want cards that relied on manual dexterity, so for the sake of both accessibility and convenience, these were banned.

Conspiracy cards

25 cards with the Conspiracy type are banned in Commander and all other formats. The full list of Conspiracy cards banned in Commander is:

Ante cards

Nine cards that reference 'playing for ante' are banned in Commander and all other formats. This is because they don't work within the rules. Playing for keeps in a four-player game is probably a bad bet anyhow. The banned MTG ante cards are:

  • Amulet of Quoz

Offensive cards

The Commander banlist includes cards that are racially or culturally insensitive. These cards have been banned in all formats, and their images were even removed from Wizards of the Coast's database in 2020. The seven cards currently included in this ban are:

  • Invoke Prejudice
  • Cleanse

Game Changers list

In 2025, Wizards of the Coast introduced a separate but linked 'Game Changers' list to the banlist conversation. Game Changers are cards that dramatically warp a game when (or shortly after) they're played. The number of game changers a deck contains is one factor in determining which Commander 'bracket' it falls into during pre-game discussions.

Though certainly not banned - or even at risk of banning - Wizards has made it clear that future banned cards are likely to come from this list. Similarly, any cards that get unbanned are likely to move onto the Game Changers list.

Wizards of the Coast last updated the Game Changers list along with the latest Commander banlist update on February 9, 2026.

Brackets explained

The beta brackets system is a tool to help Commander players talk about the gameplay experience they want to create with their deck. Each bracket has a set of deck-building conditions: if a deck meets those conditions, it sits in that bracket.

1. Exhibition

Decks prioritize theme over function and showcase a unique idea or experience over valuing winning.

  • No game changers
  • No mass land denial
  • No extra turns
  • No two-card infinite combos (game-enders, lockouts, or infinite)
  • Few tutors

2. Core

Decks are focused, even if every card choice isn't the highest power, and comparable to an average precon. Wins are often telegraphed or incremental.

  • No game changers
  • No mass land denial
  • No chaining extra turns
  • No two-card infinite combos (game-enders, lockouts, or infinite)
  • Few tutors

3. Upgraded

Decks are thoughtfully designed, full of synergistic or strong cards. Games could end out of nowhere with powerful spells and late-game combos.

  • No mass land denial
  • No chaining extra turns
  • Late game, two-card infinite combos allowed
  • Up to three game changers

4. Optimized

Decks are turbocharged with the most powerful cards in the format. Everybody intends to win and is ready to play against anything.

No restrictions other than the banlist.

5. CEDH

Decks are built to win in the competitive metagame. Players intend to use only the most powerful strategies.

  • No restrictions other than the banlist.

Are Commander brackets power levels?

Commander brackets are numbered, but these numbers don't measure the power level of a deck. The higher the bracket, the more tools the deck has to succeed in competitive, meta-focused gameplay. The lower the bracket, the more casual and focused on 'doing something neat with friends' the deck is.

Hopefully, players can use the brackets to choose decks that have similar gameplay goals. There will still be decks that perform well above or below what their bracket suggests.

You'll find a welcoming community in the free Wargamer Discord who are eager to discuss your latest deck brews with you. To make sure you don't miss the best stories on Wargamer each week, sign up to our newsletter.

title: MTG Star Trek breaks one of Magic's most infamous combos
content:
Oh good, MTG players found a way to break Food Chain! This classic combo seen in Legacy and cEDH decks is about to get even stronger, thanks to a brand new card from the Star Trek set. That card features Khan, one of the franchise's most iconic villains.

Khan, Wrathful Heart is a legendary creature that can be cast from exile, which immediately makes it an obvious choice for Food Chain decks. For those unfamiliar, this combo relies on Food Chain, alongside any creature that can be cast from exile - such as Misthollow Griffin or Squee. You keep on sacrificing those creatures to Food Chain and recasting them, with a net gain of one mana each time, allowing you to make infinite mana with which to win the game.

What makes Khan, Wrathful Heart so much better than these older options is that he has another effect. He can also turn creatures or artifacts into card draw. Traditionally, for a Food Chain cEDH deck, you've needed to run a commander that provides immediate value from entering the battlefield (be that card draw or direct damage) so you can keep casting and exiling it with your unlimited mana and have a built in way to win.

Pantlaza or Atraxa, cards that fetch up other cards on ETB, are classic examples of Food Chain commanders in this vein.

Khan provides that value all by himself, though, which means technically any deck can now be a Food Chain deck. You can't actually whiff as long as your commander is a creature, since you can sacrifice them to Khan if you don't draw anything you want to put in the bin. Remember you have infinite mana in this scenario; commander tax may as well not exist.

I'm excited to see what black-based Food Chain decks crop up around Khan, and if this widens the pool of commanders folks are using for this archetype.

title: The Pokémon TCG's first 2027 release, Flowing Fists, is revealed
content:
We finally know the name of the next Pokémon TCG set coming out after Delta Reign. That set is Flowing Fists, and it's launching on February 5, 2027. We've long known that this release will focus on Mega Lucario, specifically the new version - Mega Lucario Z - which debuted in the Pokémon Legends Z-A Mega Dimension DLC last December.

Flowing Fists is the English language counterpart to Aura Seeker, the Japanese set due to launch November 27 this year. We've already seen several of its cards, including the face card Mega Lucario, and with the set roughly a month away, we should expect The Pokémon Company to release the Japanese spoilers imminently, giving the rest of us a sneak peek at what to expect in February.

Obviously, it's the full art rares we're all looking forward to seeing, but even before we knew what this set would be called, a couple of its cards had already been shown off. As mentioned, these include Mega Lucario Z, a metal type Mega ex Pokémon with an 'Aura Seeker' ability that fetches up any Supporter from your deck. It can also easily KO weak exs, as its 120 damage attack deals twice as much to them.

However, even though it only has 210 HP, Mega Lucario Z ex still can't take down the new Sigilyph ex. That's because it has an ability that blocks all damage from mega evolutions. While this only prevents damage to itself, this wall is still likely to be a meta-shaping tool, helping to keep mega evolution decks in check. Perhaps it'll be a boon to the powerful single-prize strategies that are already performing well.

Before Flowing Fists, we still have the final Pokémon set of the year, Delta Reign, to look forward to, as it launches on November 6 - just a couple of weeks away. If you haven't already, check out the chase cards from this release, from the beautiful Raikou ex to the surprisingly pretty Kecleon.

title: Games Workshop Accidentally Leaks New Dwarf Faction for Age of Sigmar
content:
Games Workshop has a new dwarf faction headed to Age of Sigmar — and we know that because the company accidentally showed it off early.

The Khazalite Holds briefly appeared on the Irish version of the Warhammer Store website before being hastily taken down. GW hasn’t released high-resolution versions of the images, so for now fans are squinting at blurry screenshots. The company also hasn’t commented further on the leak itself.

What We Know So Far

Age of Sigmar already has two duardin factions — the steampunk air pirates of the Kharadron Overlords and the slayer-inspired Fyreslayers — but neither scratches the itch for classic Warhammer dwarves. The Khazalite Holds look set to change that.

The leaked images showed off three distinct groups of miniatures:

  • Footsoldiers — Stoic, unrelenting infantry with shields bearing traditional runes that Warhammer Fantasy veterans will recognise
  • Golem-like constructs — A trio of heavy hitters, described by one observer as “stout as all hell,” armed with greathammers and looking every bit the linebreakers
  • A leader — Thick armour, well-plaited hair, a billowing cloak, a great axe, and an impressive headpiece. Plus a tactical rock, naturally.

The models feature pseudo-Nordic knotwork and runic designs straight out of the Old World, but with the proportions and round bases that Age of Sigmar players are used to.

GW Responds to the Leak

Rather than waiting for Friday’s Big Autumn Warhammer Preview, GW leaned into the leak and shared a bit more about the faction.

“Meet a Gholem of Gazul,” the company said. “What’s a Gholem? Who is Gazul? Well, for now all we can say is that it marches to war amidst the war throngs of the Khazalites Holds – an all-new Duardin faction for Warhammer Age of Sigmar. We’ll delve into the lore, rules and even more sweet new miniatures on Friday in the live reveal show.”

So lore, rules, and more miniatures are all coming at the end of the week.

The Rumours Were Right

This one didn’t come out of nowhere. Drolf Ironhead, a hero from Warhammer Quest: Darkwater released earlier this year, had already hinted that a faction like this might be on the way. The leaked web images confirmed what fans had been speculating about for months.

Why Fans Are Excited

For longtime Warhammer players, this feels like a homecoming. The Old World’s classic dwarves have been missing from Age of Sigmar, and the Khazalite Holds look like a proper spiritual successor — much like how the Lumineth Realm-lords gave High Elf fans a new home in the Mortal Realms.

The full reveal is expected at Friday’s live show.
